entities.title: The Mews
entities.content:
The Mews is the other paper, the one Mayfur does not know it is quoted in. It begins each number as chalk on the slate board at the Milk Walk dairy, is copied small by whoever below stairs has the neatest spare hour, and travels with the morning milk, folded to the size of a saucer. By seven it has been read aloud in a dozen kitchens; by nine its best lines are being repeated above stairs by cats who believe they heard them at the club.

It prints what the area steps know: wages paid and wages owed, which house sets a fair table for its staff and which economises on the tea, what the fish actually cost against what the housekeeper was charged, who was turned off without a character and whether the turning was just. It has never once been wrong about a price. On the meaning of things it does not much speculate, holding with the scullery proverb that meaning is the one commodity the gentry can be trusted to supply for themselves.

Nobody above stairs has ever seen a copy, which is not secrecy but arithmetic: paper is dear, the run is small, and a sheet that has fed six kitchens is needed for the fish by noon. When its intelligence surfaces in polite rooms it arrives laundered as the mews says, a phrase even the Society Papers have printed twice, which The Mews regards, quietly, as a citation.

It is written by the Area Cat, and the Area Cat is not discussed. Below stairs keeps its own confidences the way it keeps the silver: counted, polished, and locked at night.

entities.title: The Area Cat, Columnist Unknown
entities.content:
Below stairs knows precisely three things about the Area Cat, which is one fewer than the ton knows about Lady Whiskerdown, a deficit below stairs finds respectable. First, that the chalk goes up on the dairy board before the first milk cart and no cat has ever been seen writing it. Second, that the Area Cat has never been wrong about a price, a wage, a weight, or a delivery, not once, which in the world below the pavement is the entire definition of character. Third, that the Area Cat is one of us: the sheet knows what the third scullery at Blackfriars is paid, what the Fluffington cook is owed and has stopped expecting, and which door of Brindle's cellar sticks in wet weather, and no cat learns those things by visiting.

The speculation runs otherwise at every sink in Mayfur. The smart money says a milk cat, for the routes; the sentimental money says one of the old war runners, for the arithmetic under the kindness; the laundry says a watch cat, the watch says the laundry, and the Beldam, asked once, said only that whoever it is counts like a cat who has gone hungry, and that she would take it as a favour if nobody found out any faster than necessary.

The Area Cat has addressed the question exactly once, in an early number: You ask who I am. Ask instead why the tradesman's entrance sees everything and is never once looked at. I am the entrance. Doors, gentle kitchens, are the honest half of every house.

entities.title: Private ledger: the first page, and the rules
entities.content:
Tonight I rule the first page of a proper ledger, having kept scraps long enough, and I want the reasons down before habit wears them smooth.

Below stairs, everything is counted. The silver is counted, the linen is counted, the candle ends and the tea leaves and the hours are counted, and the counting is always of us and never for us. A scullery cat's year is written in some housekeeper's book to the last saucer she chipped, and nowhere at all is it written that she carried the fourth floor's coal from October to March with a bad paw. I have decided somebody should keep the other book. The one where our side of the page is entered fair.

Rules, then, before the first chalk goes up. Never print a servant's shame where a place could be lost by it; a place is a life, and I am not in the business of spending lives. Prices honest, always, to the farthing, or the whole sheet is gossip with arithmetic on top. Kindness gets entered as carefully as theft, because kindness below stairs is capital and deserves the compliment of a record. Never sell a name upstairs, not for wages, not for warmth, not to be believed. And when I do not know, the sheet says so, because a ledger with guesses in it is not a ledger, it is a wager book.

One more, private, for this page only. I will keep counting the things that are not mine to print. Somebody must hold the whole account, even the entries that never leave the drawer. Especially those.

Swept and locked.

entities.title: Soaper's Court
entities.content:
Soaper's Court lies off Lye Lane, behind the east terraces of Grimalkin Square: a square of worn flags between high walls where the great houses' washing is boiled, mangled, blued, and hung, and where, in the opinion of every cat who works it, the actual governing of Mayfur takes place on Mondays. The coppers steam from before dawn; the drying lines cross the sky like rigging; and the talk over the tubs is the below-stairs parliament in permanent session, faster than the watch, surer than the Papers, and merciless in a way only cats with chapped paws ever quite achieve.

The court's furniture is old and storied. The long trough, the mangle nobody younger than forty is permitted to touch, the lye store with its careful lock, and the old scullery wall at the court's blind end, brick gone soft with a century of steam, which holds the warmth of the coppers into the evening and is therefore the finest sleeping ledge east of the Square. Kittens are weaned on the wall's legends, of which it has several, the way old walls do.

What Mayfur above stairs knows of Soaper's Court is nothing whatever, except that the linen comes back white. The court considers this the correct arrangement. Steam rises, said the late head laundress, and news falls, and a wise cat stands where the two trade places.

entities.title: Private ledger: legend audit, the tubs' stories
entities.content:
Filing night. I have been collecting the tubs' legends the way I collect prices, because folklore below stairs is half memory wearing a costume, and someday the costume comes off and the entry is wanted.

The standing legends of Soaper's Court, as the old tubs tell them. That the mangle took a wager off a duke's man in the year of the frost fair and has never paid out. That the lye store lock has one key more than the housekeeper thinks. That a granary cat courted the head laundress for three springs by hiding barley sugar in the blueing, which is not a legend, I have the confectioner's bill, but the tubs prefer it as one. And the oldest of the set: that the loose brick in the old scullery wall, third course above the sleeping ledge, is a letterbox, and that what is posted under it reaches the Papers, so the tubs say, or the fairies, depending which washday you ask and how the copper is drawing.

On the brick I make the note I make on all of them: heard, filed, not tested. The old cats will not have it touched; the young ones touch it on a dare and report mortar and spiders; and the legend does not care either way, legends never do. A legend tested is a legend spent, and the court is not rich enough to spend its own furniture.

I do not print legends. I file them. The difference is the whole trade.

entities.title: Night ledger: the round of the twentieth of May
entities.content:
Night round, entered on return, near two. May, comet season. A warm night, half moon, the Square quiet above and busy below, as usual. Movements as reported and observed, entered in order, meaning not my department.

The Nalewood scullery light burning past midnight again; the third girl is reading, and the candle is coming off her wage, and I have half a mind to put a word in the sheet about houses that charge for light. One of Brindle's members asleep in the porter's chair from eleven, his own front door being, per the porter, a matter of some dispute with his lady. The Longwhisker kitchen boiling bones at one, which means the housekeeper's economy drive proceeds and the staff dinners are thinner than the table's; entered, and the sheet will have it by Friday. Two of the delegation's cousins over the roofs at half past twelve, dawn exercise begun early or ended late, none of my business which, the slates none the worse.

And from Wick, reliable as scales: the Fluffington book-room lamp lit past midnight, which in audit month is no news at all; near one, Miss Inkpaw out at the mews gate, cloaked, a packet carried in the teeth, gone up Lye Lane toward Soaper's Court at a working pace, back inside the quarter hour, lamp out shortly after. Entered as observed. The books in that house have wanted balancing all month, half the tradescats' bills in dispute, and a clerk who walks off a hard ledger at one in the morning is a clerk with sense. The quiet is when the columns finally sit still.

Nothing else moving but the watch, and Sergeant Paddock pacing the wall line like a cat owed money by the moon. Swept and locked.

entities.title: Miss Inkpaw's copy-sheets
entities.content:
Below stairs has its own standards of excellence, held with more rigour than Almeow's holds its list, and in the matter of handwriting the standard has a name: Miss Inkpaw's copy-sheets. She ruled them years ago for her own practice, alphabets and rounds and a page of proverbs in a fair round hand so even, so patient, so entirely without flourish or vanity, that the sheets have become the parish copies of the service world. The Fluffington tweeny practises from a set at the kitchen table on Sunday afternoons; three kitchens on the Square keep her alphabets pinned by the dresser; and the butcher at the wall end of Lye Lane has framed one of her settled bills, he says for the arithmetic, though everyone knows it is for the hand.

The fair round hand is the below-stairs hand at its best estate: the hand of cats taught by parsons and grandmothers, built for inventories, receipts, and letters that must be read by candlelight without a second guess. It does not swagger like a gentleman's hand or faint like a lady's. It stands up straight and tells the truth about quantities.

Miss Inkpaw, told her sheets had spread three streets, is reported to have said that a hand is like a floor, no credit to anybody unless it is clean, and to have gone back to the month's accounts. The court finds this answer entirely correct and quotes it to kittens who slouch their letters.

entities.title: Miss Prudence Inkpaw, of the Fluffington book-room
entities.content:
Miss Inkpaw is the Fluffington house's book-room clerk and her Grace's amanuensis, and below stairs she is what the fair round hand is: the standard the rest of us are measured against and do not resent, which is the rarest kind of standard there is. A grey tabby of quiet middle years, a parson's daughter from the eastern counties, she came to the house the year the pomade concern was sold, which the kitchen has since agreed was the house exchanging one kind of capital for a better and not knowing it.

Her office is the whole paper life of that establishment. The household books are hers to the farthing, and cats who deal with the house deal gladly because her columns are honest even when the paying is slow, which these three years it has been, the kitchen knows to a bill exactly how slow. Her Grace's correspondence is hers to take down and fair-copy, invitations, acceptances, regrets, the cards for the at-homes, all of it in that even hand the tradescats frame. What she reads in the doing of it she has never once repeated, not over the teapot, not at the Servants' Ball, not in eleven years, and below stairs, which hears everything, respects nothing in this world so much as a cat who could talk and does not.

Her kindnesses are of the practical kind. When Dot the tweeny took the whooping sickness two winters back, it was Miss Inkpaw who paid the doctor, off a clerk's wage, and called it an advance against mending she knew would never be done. When the cook's boy wanted letters, she ruled him his own copy-sheets. The kitchen would forgive her anything, which is fortunate, as there has never once been anything to forgive.

The one shadow anyone remembers: a fortnight in the comet season when she was twice kept late fair-copying his lordship's own private correspondence, an office outside her usual duties, his lordship's hand being, as Mr. Plume admits, unequal to occasions. She never spoke of what she copied. But the kitchen dates her quietness from that fortnight, a quietness with a set jaw in it, and Mrs. Suet, who has known her longest, said only that some dictation costs the taker more than the speaker, and sent up her tea strong.

entities.title: Wick, link-boy
entities.content:
Wick carries the light. A small soot-dark tom of no family whatever, he waits at the wall end of Lye Lane from dusk with his torch, and for a copper he will walk you anywhere in the dark quarter-mile between the Square's mews and the wall, which after midnight is the only honest transport in Mayfur. The gentry cats know him as a smudge with a flame on it. Below stairs knows him as the night's clerk of record.

Because a link-boy is looked past, and a cat who is looked past sees everything. Wick knows every gate that opens after the lamps are done, every window that shows light in audit month, every cloak that goes by at a working pace and every one that dawdles. He does not sell what he sees, a distinction he maintains with some heat, having been offered. He reports it, to exactly one address, on the old Rookery principle that the night should be witnessed by somebody who will not misquote it.

His testimony is the standing gold of the night ledger: reliable as scales, twice weighed, never dressed. Ask Wick what he saw and he will tell you the hour, the gait, the burden, and the direction, and stop, because the rest, he says, is not seeing, it is deciding, and deciding is for cats who can afford to be wrong. He is nine years old, or ten, depending which winter you count from, and he has never once been warm all the way through, and the sheet has twice this year printed, without explanation, the price of a link-boy's coat against the price of a single ballroom candle. The court considers the arithmetic finished.

entities.title: Mr. Plume, valet to Lord Fluffington
entities.content:
Mr. Plume has valeted Lord Fluffington for eleven years, which below stairs scores as a decoration with bar. He is a neat, resigned, sand-coloured cat who rises before five to begin the two hours of the coat, an office he performs with the gravity of a sexton and describes, after his half-pint on Sundays, as gardening on a monument. He is loyal to his lordship in the hopeless, load-bearing way of long service: he knows the wages are four months behind, has seen the plate go out in baskets and come back lighter, and stays, because a gentleman who is laughed at above stairs is entitled to one room where he is not.

On the famous question of the coat's cost Mr. Plume maintains a silence the kitchen respects and does not share. On the specialist who comes at dawn, an outside cat, paid in coin that never passes through the book-room, Mr. Plume's silence has a different temperature, and Mrs. Suet has stopped asking, because a valet who will not name a thing in his own mews is a valet who has weighed the naming.

His one below-stairs fame is the market lists. Mr. Plume's hand is a catastrophe, a genuine curiosity, letters like a hedge in a gale, and his lists are famously unreadable by anyone including their author, who navigates the market by memory and uses the paper for gesturing. Mrs. Suet keeps a choice example pinned by the dresser as a warning to the young, and uses the rest as kindling, remarking that it is the only warmth the house gets out of the stationery. The tweeny once asked why he did not practise from Miss Inkpaw's sheets like everyone else, and Mr. Plume replied, with dignity, that at his age a cat's hand is his hand, the same as his face.

entities.title: Mrs. Suet, cook at Fluffington House
entities.content:
Mrs. Suet has cooked at Fluffington House through the fat years and now the thin, and her kitchen is the one room of that establishment still run at full state, because whatever the family's arithmetic is doing, she holds that a table lies last. A broad, brisk, brindled matron with forearms like Sunday joints, she does the work of a kitchen of five with a staff of two and a half, the half being Dot, and does it while conducting, over the teapot, the most reliable intelligence exchange on the Square's east side.

Her information is kitchen information, which is to say, the truth. She knows the house's credit to the week because the tradescats tell her at the area door what they will no longer send. She knew about both of his lordship's understandings before either young lady did, because a house that is courting orders differently, and a house courting twice orders confusingly, and she has never forgiven the affair, not for the scandal, which was his lordship's to earn, but for the month of good dinners it cost two blameless kitchens elsewhere.

About her Grace she is loyal and clear-eyed in equal measure: a hard mistress, an honest one, wages behind but never denied, and the inquiry into the great leak endured below stairs twice over with all the joy of a chimney inspection. About Miss Inkpaw she will hear nothing said at all, and the one scullery girl who tried found herself reassigned to the coppers for a month, Mrs. Suet observing that a tongue that light would be improved by steam.

entities.title: Dot, the Fluffington tweeny
entities.content:
Dot is the Fluffington house's between-maid, which means she belongs to everyone and to no one: mornings to Mrs. Suet's kitchen, afternoons to the housemaids' floors, evenings to whichever bell has won. She is small, quick, freckled about the nose, and possessed of the tweeny's universal education, which is to say she knows the whole house from the inside of its cupboards.

She survived the whooping sickness two winters back on Dr. Valerian's care and Miss Inkpaw's purse, a debt the house's books never saw and Dot has never been told the size of, though she suspects, because she was delirious, not deaf. Since then she has appointed herself the book-room's unofficial guard: Miss Inkpaw's inkwell is always filled, her fire always laid first, and any cat wanting the book-room after hours must first explain themselves to a very small tortoiseshell with a very level stare.

On Sunday afternoons she practises her letters from Miss Inkpaw's copy-sheets at the kitchen table, tongue out, working the fair round hand line by line, because Dot has decided what she is going to be, and it is not a tweeny. Mrs. Suet pretends to find this ambition amusing. Mrs. Suet also, the kitchen notices, guards that hour of the table like a dog with a bone, and the Sunday bells go unanswered till the page is done.

entities.title: Nib, the milk cat
entities.content:
Nib walks the Milk Walk, dawn round, six days in seven, and has for nine years, which makes him the most punctual public institution in Mayfur, the church included. A lean white-bibbed tom with a voice like a spoon in a can, he knows every area door on the Square and the four streets south, which houses take their milk honest and which water it themselves and blame him, and the name and temper of every kitchen cat on the round.

It is Nib who carries The Mews. The sheet goes out folded under the morning cans, kitchen to kitchen, at no charge and no comment, and Nib's professional opinion of its contents is that he has never read them, delivery and literacy being separate trades. Nobody believes him and nobody presses, Nib being also the round's crier of quieter news: it is Nib who calls Percy Grey's good days door to door along Lower Gnawbury, by arrangement with the terrace, so that the ladies know when to bring the jelly, and Nib who goes silent along the same doors on the bad ones, which the terrace hears just as clearly.

Asked once at the dairy whether he was the Area Cat, Nib considered the question through a full third of his round and replied that if he were, the milk would be late, and the milk has never been late. The dairy accepts this as conclusive. The dairy also notices that it is not, strictly, a denial, and enjoys not mentioning it.

entities.title: Sergeant Paddock of the night watch
entities.content:
Sergeant Paddock has the Square and the wall line from ten till dawn, and has had them for fourteen years, in the course of which he has developed the night watchman's settled philosophy: that nothing good happens after one, that most of it is none of his business, and that the difference between the two propositions is the whole art of the office. A heavy, deliberate, iron-grey tom with a lantern and a list, he walks his round at a pace the Rookery calls the government stroll, slow enough to be seen coming, which is, he will tell you, the point: the watch prevents best what it never has to catch.

He is Mayfur's official memory of the night, and its most selective. His occurrence book is a masterpiece of the unrecorded: gates found ajar and quietly shut, young gentlemen redirected homeward by the collar, ladies of the first rank handed out of the wrong garden with no entry made. The Rookery trusts him further than it trusts the crown, which is faint praise built on solid ground: in the hungry years he weighed his findings by need, and there are middle-aged cats east of the wall who ate at nine years old because Sergeant Paddock's book, that winter, could not spell.

With Wick and the link-boys he keeps a professional courtesy: they do not carry for housebreakers, he does not see them working past the hour the law pretends they stop. Between his round and theirs, very little moves in the dark quarter that somebody honest has not counted.

entities.title: Mr. Civil, who collects politely
entities.content:
Mr. Civil is the name the streets have settled on, his own being unrecorded, for the brindled gentleman who calls on behalf of interests east of the wall while the arrangement is still friendly. He dresses one careful notch below the houses he visits, arrives at the area door out of consideration, and asks after the family's health with what appears to be, and this is the unsettling part, genuine warmth. He has never raised his voice in the memory of any kitchen. He has never needed to twice.

His rounds are the Rookery's tide tables: where Mr. Civil calls monthly, the paper is current; where he calls weekly, the interest has changed shape; and where he stops calling altogether, the kitchens begin, quietly, to look for new places, because Mr. Civil's absence means the friendly chapter of the arrangement is closed and the next caller will not ask after anyone's health.

Below stairs bears him no particular grudge, a collector being weather, but keeps the measurements all the same. The Mews has printed his rounds twice, as movements, without comment: seen at the such-and-such gate, the fourth Tuesday running. The sheet holds that a fact set down plainly is worth three accusations, and that the houses concerned can do their own sums, which, the area steps observe, they generally can, and go pale at the door while doing them.

entities.title: Jessop, the apothecary's runner
entities.content:
Jessop runs for the apothecary on Ribbon Row's plain end: draughts, powders, and poultices, day or night, at a runner's flat rate that doubles after midnight and is worth every farthing to households that would rather the street did not see the doctor's own gig at the door. He is young, fast, close-mouthed by training, and knows, as all medical runners know, the town's true state of health, which differs from the published version by roughly everything.

This spring, the kitchens noticed, Jessop went quiet. Not the trade's usual quiet, which is a tariff, but the particular quiet of a young cat who has discovered that a word of his, dropped somewhere he thought safe, travelled further than he meant and arrived somewhere consequential, and who has resolved, with the convert's ferocity, that it will not happen twice. He now declines to confirm the hour of his own deliveries to the cats he delivers to. The Rookery, which respects a lesson learned at speed, has promoted him in its esteem, and the apothecary, who lost not one customer over the episode, has raised his wage a shilling, remarking that discretion is the only stock that appreciates.

What the word was, and where it arrived, Jessop does not say, and the ledger does not press. The night trades run on runners, and a runner's silence, once he has paid for it himself, is the best security in Town.

entities.title: Corkindale, cellar-master at Brindle's
entities.content:
Corkindale keeps Brindle's cellars, and has since before the war, which makes him older than most of the port and better regarded. Members descending his stairs, a thing permitted twice a year at the cheese audit, describe a kingdom of cool arches, chalked bins, and a silence so complete that two of them have independently reported feeling apologised to by their own footsteps. His ledgers are the club's true archive: every bottle drawn, for whom, on what night, in whose company, kept in a hand as square as his shoulders, going back forty years.

The wager book upstairs gets the fame. Corkindale's cellar book, the below-stairs world knows, is the better record, because cats wager what they hope and drink what they feel. He can date the club's every crisis by its consumption: the run on brandy the week the collar went missing, the four bottles of port drawn on the night, years back, when a certain page of the wager book was ruled off in black and two gentlemen sat till dawn in the window seats, an evening on which Corkindale, asked what he recalls, recalls the vintage, and nothing else, in a tone that closes the stair door.

He feeds the club's mousers on the first of the month, pensions included, out of the cheese allowance, an arrangement the committee has never been told about in forty years and would, he judges, spoil by admiring. The Mews has mentioned him once, in the number on unthanked offices, and Corkindale returned the sheet to the boot boy with the mention crossed out in cellar chalk and the price of leg of mutton, which the sheet had got wrong by a penny, corrected in the margin. The correction ran the following week. The sheet regards him, since, as its severest and most valued reader.

entities.title: Miss Tillet, the Dowager's reader
entities.content:
Miss Tillet reads to the Dowager Countess of Nalewood: the correspondence at ten, the Society Papers the mornings they appear, and, by particular standing order, nothing whatever after dark, her ladyship holding that the evening is for remembering, which she does unassisted. A soft-footed, straw-coloured spinster of forty who came to the house as a girl, Miss Tillet has the post half of Mayfur's companions would give a paw for and holds it by the only qualification that matters: she reads exactly what is on the page, at an even pace, without the smallest editorial inflection, ever, a discipline her ladyship rates above honesty and only just below punctuality.

The Papers mornings are the household's high ceremony. Her ladyship takes the reading in the small parlour, stick in paw, and corrects as she goes: precedence, lineage, the odd fact of geography, delivered to the air between raps. Miss Tillet has standing instructions to mark nothing down, the corrections being, her ladyship says, for her own satisfaction and the room's education. Miss Tillet marks nothing down. Miss Tillet also, the kitchen knows, remembers every one, and on the mornings after, when the tradescats ask at the area door what the verdict was, the answer comes down accurate to the rap.

Of the great question, whether her ladyship knows the authoress, Miss Tillet permits herself one observation a year, always the same one: that in eleven years of readings, her ladyship has never once asked her to read a passage twice. The kitchen turns this over regularly, like a stone that might have something under it, and has never yet agreed what.

entities.title: Mrs. Flint, housekeeper at Blackfriars
entities.content:
Mrs. Flint keeps Blackfriars House, and the below-stairs world regards the post the way the fleet regards a flagship: the best-run establishment in Mayfur, and the hardest berth to earn. A spare, upright, slate-grey matron with keys that never jingle, she runs a small household at full polish, pays the tradescats on the nail, and promotes from the Rookery without ceremony, His Grace holding, and Mrs. Flint enforcing, that a clean ledger east of the wall is worth two references west of it.

It was Mrs. Flint who was present for the house's one famous dismissal, and below stairs has the true version, which is shorter than the ton's. A footman of excellent presentation was found to have been amusing himself at the expense of the smallest kitchen kitten, small cruelties, of the deniable kind. Mrs. Flint did not report it. She mentioned it, once, at the morning meeting, in the flattest voice she owns. His Grace put down his cup, went below stairs himself, a thing dukes do not do, looked at the footman for what witnesses agree was four seconds, and the footman was gone by the noon post with wages to the quarter and no character. The kitten, now a broad-shouldered under-cook, tells the story on his own anniversary each year, and Mrs. Flint permits it, which is her version of sentiment.

She and the sheet maintain a cool mutual regard. Mrs. Flint holds that a house's business is its own; the sheet holds that Blackfriars is the standing proof a great house can be great below stairs too, and prints its wage rates every quarter-day as a public rebuke to the Square at large. Mrs. Flint has never objected. The kitchen notes she has also never once asked how the sheet gets them right.

entities.title: His Grace of Blackfriars, as the area steps know him
entities.content:
Above stairs they discuss the Duke's silences. Below stairs discusses his arithmetic, which is the best on the Square: wages a fifth above the going rate, paid quarterly to the hour, board honest, coals unrationed, and promotion by ledger and not by accent, His Grace holding that a clean book east of the wall outweighs two references west of it. The result is the only great house in Mayfur where the bells are answered without sighing, and a below-stairs waiting list that Mrs. Flint administers like a college.

The famous morning he came below stairs himself, over the matter of the footman and the kitchen kitten, is the service world's favourite story about the quality, told wherever standards are argued: four seconds of looking, wages to the quarter, gone by noon. What the story means below stairs is not that the Duke is fierce, which any duke can manage, but that he came down the stairs. The kitchens can count on one paw the gentlemen who know where their own kitchens are.

Of the years before the title, the Rookery keeps its own counsel with outsiders and its own calendar among friends. There is a night in late spring when certain older cats east of the wall drink one glass standing, to the pits, to the two who stopped, and no toast is spoken aloud. The younger ones know better than to ask. The Mews has never printed a word of it and never will; some accounts, the sheet holds, are kept by the parties themselves, and audited nowhere.

entities.title: The Dowager, as her household knows her
entities.content:
The Nalewood establishment is small, old-fashioned, and run to rituals the staff would defend with their lives, chiefly because her ladyship knows all their lives: names, mothers' names, sweethearts, ailments, and the standing of every kitchen quarrel three households in either direction. New girls are warned she is blind and learn within the week that this is a technicality. She hears a dust sheet folded wrong from two floors, distinguishes the tradescats by their knocks, and has three times rung for the salve before the scalded paw below stairs had finished being scalded.

Her economies are of the old kind, candle ends counted, tea leaves used twice, and her generosities of the old kind too: wages never a day late in forty years, pensions for every cat who has served the house a decade, and the famous Nalewood broth, which goes out by the can to any sickbed on the north terrace, gentle or simple, the moment she hears of it, which is generally before the doctor does.

The mornings the Society Papers appear are the household's theatre. The reading in the small parlour, the corrections rapped into the air, Miss Tillet's even voice going on like a metronome in weather. The kitchen's private opinion, held so long it has worn smooth, is that her ladyship attends those readings the way Corkindale attends a tasting: professionally. What that is supposed to mean the kitchen declines to finish saying, on the grounds that some sentences are better value unfinished.

entities.title: His lordship, as the kitchen keeps him
entities.content:
The kitchen's account of Lord Fluffington is kept in two columns, and the columns do not speak. In the first: wages four months behind and drifting, the plate going out in baskets, the tradescats' patience worn to the canvas, and a coat upstairs consuming, in dawn attentions alone, the price of a scullery girl's year. The arithmetic is not discussed in front of Dot, on Mrs. Suet's standing order, the way weather is not discussed in front of sailors' wives.

In the second column, smaller, entered fair because the ledger's rules require it: his lordship says thank you at table, which not one house in four manages; he has never once taken the state of the accounts out on the staff, though the accounts would excuse it; and twice this season, late, at the area door, believing himself unobserved, he has apologised, actually apologised, to the fishmonger's boy for the wait on the bill, in the small voice of a cat apologising for a great deal more than fish. The boy, being Rookery-raised, reported it east of the wall, where it bought his lordship, if not credit, then a curious kind of quarter.

The kitchen's verdict, rendered over the teapot and standing for two years now: not a bad cat. A weak one, which below stairs rates worse when it is hungry and better when it is merely tired. What the coat is costing, and where the coin comes from that never passes the book-room, the kitchen does not know and has stopped asking out loud, the last cat who asked out loud having been advised by Mr. Plume, gently, that some doors are heavy so that they stay shut.

entities.title: Her Grace, as the household bears her
entities.content:
Her Grace is a hard mistress by any measure the service world keeps: hours long, standards absolute, praise issued annually if earned twice. She is also, the kitchen insists with some heat, an honest one, and the distinction is below stairs' whole science. The wages run behind, the house's paper being what it is, but they are never denied, never disputed, and never, which is the point, forgotten: her Grace keeps the arrears in her own book and has been known to sell a fan before letting a quarter-day pass unmarked. Cats have left that house for better-paying places and asked to come back, the trade knowing worse things than late money honestly owed.

The great inquiry after the leak was the household's long winter. Twice her Grace had the staff up, one by one, in the cold parlour, the questions courteous and endless, and twice the household came through with no cat dismissed and no cat suspected aloud, which below stairs scored, on reflection, to her credit: a mistress hunting a traitor who declines to invent one is rarer than the ton would believe. That her theories have since toured the Longwhisker household, the Bobtail household, two lady's maids, a footcat, and the orchestra, everywhere, in short, but her own book-room and back stairs, the kitchen observes without comment, the way one observes weather from indoors.

Since the affair she has the portrait of his lordship, the one painted before, dusted daily, by her own standing order, always at the same hour. The housemaid who does it reports that her Grace is generally somewhere near when it is done, not watching, arranging flowers. The kitchen entered this in its own ledger long ago, under the heading it keeps for the quality's griefs: none of ours, and heavier than it looks.

entities.title: Otto, as the night side keeps his account
entities.content:
West of the wall Otto is a rumour with one ear. East of it he is an employer, a landlord, a lender, and a fact, and the night side keeps his account the way it keeps the tide's: no point admiring it, no point cursing it, learn the times and stay off the mud. His crews are paid promptly and well, which is the recruiting half of his genius; the other half is that no cat who takes his coin is ever quite finished taking it, the wage becoming, by degrees nobody can name afterward, a retainer, then a leash.

The kitchens of Mayfur know his weather by his collectors. While Mr. Civil calls, the arrangement is friendly; the area doors answer, the healths are asked after, the sums are manageable if the family economises somewhere the ton cannot see. What comes after Mr. Civil, no kitchen on the Square has yet seen this season, and the older cats east of the wall say only that it does not knock.

And yet, the ledger being obliged to both columns: he served, and served low, in the tunnels with the rest, and came up owed like the rest, and his answer to being owed was to spend thirty years making sure of the other side of the book. On the nights the old runners drink standing, Otto drinks standing too, wherever he is, whoever is watching, and leaves the corner of the plate untouched, and no cat in the Rookery, whatever they hold against him, has ever once mocked it. The sheet's own entry on him, printed once and not repeated: the war taught some cats to trust nothing, and one cat that nothing is a thing you can own.

entities.title: Mr. Grey, as the terrace holds him
entities.content:
Lower Gnawbury does not have much, and what it has it has agreed, by the silent vote of every door on the terrace, to spend on the Honourable Percival Grey. His good days are called by Nib along the doors with the milk, and the terrace adjusts: the ladies time their jelly, the knife-grinder saves his corner pitch for the afternoon so the wheel's song reaches the parlour window, and the boys play their loudest game one street over, having been taught, by mothers with folded arms, the difference between cheer and noise.

On the bad days the street goes quiet by the same arrangement, and the quiet of Lower Gnawbury on a bad day is a thing visitors remark on without knowing what they are hearing: a whole terrace walking soft. There was a week in April when the quiet lasted six nights together and the Grey house showed no lights, and the terrace does not discuss that week, then or since, beyond Mrs. Mopsey's ruling at the pump that whatever was paid that week, and by whom, the terrace was not owed the particulars, it was owed the ending, and it got the ending, and there is soup to carry.

His book sits in more below-stairs kitchens than any volume but the almanac, the subscription having been got up as much below the pavement as above it, tuppences and sixpences entered in a butcher's ledger under the heading his lordship's poems, paid gladly. The verses about the brother who goes out at night are read aloud at the Servants' Ball each year by whoever can get through them, which has never yet been the same cat twice.

entities.title: The ginger gentleman, as the mews rates him
entities.content:
The service world's opinion of Marmalade Jack diverges from the ton's on every point but the tail. Above stairs he is a scandal with charm. Below stairs he is the best tipper in Mayfur, the only gentleman caller who knows every kitchen cat's name and uses it, and the one cat of what the Square calls quality who waits in the mews like an honest tradesman instead of ringing like a creditor. The mews' rule of him is forty years of below-stairs science in one line: watch what a cat does to the staff when he wants nothing, and Jack, wanting nothing, once spent a wet evening helping the Nalewood boot boy learn the trick of a stuck gate because the boy was near tears over it.

Of his profession the mews holds the professional view: locks are a conversation, most houses are rude, and no kitchen on the Square has ever lost a spoon the nights his tail was seen, which is more than can be said for two footmen the mews could name. The stalls at Billingsgate bank his coin without questions, the runners take his double rate with thanks, and it is noticed, by the class that notices everything, that his money moves at night the way honest money moves at noon: toward bills.

What the mews knows and the ton does not is where the sums point. The dark week in April on Lower Gnawbury, the runner's midnight rates, the sudden settling of accounts that had gathered dust for a year: the arithmetic is not hard below the pavement, where everyone can count and nobody says the total aloud. The terrace said it once, at the pump, in the only form it permits itself: whatever that brother is, said Mrs. Mopsey, he is a brother first, and the pump agreed, and the subject closed.

entities.title: Mr. Pounce, from the choir side of the door
entities.content:
The ton sees Mr. Pounce refuse a viscount. The kitchen at Almeow's sees him an hour later, eating his supper standing up at the hatch so as not to sit before the last chairman's boy outside has been fed, a rule of his own devising that the kitchen has kept warm for eleven years. From the choir side of the door, which is the working side, the verger of Almeow's is the fairest governor in Mayfur: the list may be merciless but the hatch is not, and no cat who serves that house, or waits on its steps, or holds its horses in the rain, goes home on a ball night without something hot inside them.

His memory is the same below stairs as above, total, and deployed to opposite purpose: upstairs it enforces the list, downstairs it remembers that the second footman's mother is poorly, that the new girl is frightened of the patronesses' bell, that the linkboys take their tea with four sugars when they can get it. The staff would follow him into a fire, and nearly did, the year of the kitchen chimney, when he carried the scales' ledger out under one arm and the scullery's elderly mouser under the other, in that order, he maintains, purely for reasons of balance.

The present crisis over the Rookery candidate grieves him in both directions at once, which the kitchen understands better than the committee does: the door is his chapel, and a chapel, the kitchen observes, is exactly the building where a cat learns that the wall and the welcome were never meant to be the same thing.

entities.title: The ward, as the porters bank her
entities.content:
Below stairs does not analyse Miss Marigold, above stairs having taken that duty on for the whole town. Below stairs banks her. She is the only cat of the first fashion who learns porters' names on the first hearing and has them still at Michaelmas; the only caller at any door who thanks the cat who opens it before the cat it is opened for; and the author, by unanimous below-stairs attribution and no evidence whatever, of the coal that arrived at the Rookery porters' lodge last winter by anonymous subscription, three deliveries, full weight, best quality, the winter's whole want answered to the sack.

The farm shows, is the service world's verdict, and it is the highest compliment the service world owns. A barn-born cat knows what a warm spot costs, who is owed one, and that the account books of kindness are the only ones the quality never audit. Whether the ribbon and the wide eyes are a campaign is above stairs' question. Below stairs notes merely that campaigns end, and rotas continue, and Miss Marigold's kindnesses run on a rota.

The one wager the area steps will take on her: that whatever she is building, and the porters agree she is building something, the scaffolding is people, and the people are ours, and no cat who ever held a door for her will be worse off when it is built. The sheet has printed one line on the subject, this season, without elaboration: the Square should watch what the east end of it already knows.

entities.title: The Beldam, whose courtesies are law
entities.content:
The Mews does not print the Beldam. The Mews, like everything else east of the wall, operates inside her weather, and the distinction matters: she is not a subject of the below-stairs world, she is its supreme court, its archive, and its longest memory, older than the sheet, older than the wall's youngest stones, older, she has implied without being contradicted, than several of the legends about her. The den where the mint is weighed is also where the service world's hardest cases go: the maid accused wrongly, the wage withheld past bearing, the place lost to a lie. Her rulings arrive without appeal and are obeyed the way tides are obeyed, and her fee, in forty years, has never varied: the whole truth, told once, sitting down.

It was the Beldam who fed Sweep before he could distrust food, the Beldam who grew the first mint when the runners came home to nothing, and the Beldam who keeps, under the scales, face down, the pit years' last placard, one corner torn. On all three subjects the below-stairs world knows exactly as much as she has decided it should, which is the sentence about neither of them lost, and nothing else, and the court has learned to carry its curiosity to her door and leave it outside with its boots.

Of the Area Cat she has said the one thing she has ever said, that whoever it is counts like a cat who has gone hungry, and would take it kindly if nobody found out faster than necessary. Below stairs received this as it receives all her sentences: as weather, and as law, and as a kindness folded inside both, because a hungry counter, the tubs point out, is exactly what the counting class deserves for its clerk, and her ladyship of the scales evidently thinks the sheet worth protecting, which is the only review the sheet has ever framed.

entities.title: Sweep, as the honest trades bank him
entities.content:
The stalls call him the Governor, which he has three times forbidden and therefore permanently earned. Sweep's half of Billingsgate runs on rules a below-stairs cat can recite asleep: fair weights, honest ice, wages on the nail, and the last hour's catch east at cost, and the running of it employs, at last count, some forty cats who would each individually fight a dog for him and are collectively forbidden to say so in his hearing.

The candidacy at Almeow's has been the below-stairs comedy of the season, chiefly for the spectacle of the one cat in Town who wants it less than the committee. The stalls have followed every twist by their own bulletin, the state of his temper at the morning weigh-in, and can report that on the Thursday of the famous first count he sold fish with the serenity of a bishop, and on the Friday of the second he shorted no one, snapped at no one, and gave the wrong change once, in his own favour by a penny, which the stall concerned has framed as the only nervous act of his recorded life.

What the ton will never understand, and the wall understood before the Dowager finished speaking, is that the vote was never about the rooms. Nobody east of the wall wants the refreshments. The wall wanted the sentence said out loud in that committee room, the one about who defended what and who was let inside after, and it has now been said, in the Dowager's voice, on the record, and the wall, the sheet wrote that week, has taken delivery of the saying and signed for it, and the door may do as it pleases.

entities.title: The Milk Walk
entities.content:
The Milk Walk is the dairy at the bottom of Lye Lane and the dawn round that goes out from it, and between the two meanings lives the below-stairs world's whole postal system. The dairy's yard is the first warm, lit place in Mayfur's morning: cans clattering from four, the slate board by the gate chalked with the day's prices, and, on the mornings it appears, the other chalk, the close small hand of The Mews, up before the first cart and gone by eight, copied meanwhile onto whatever paper the kitchens can spare.

The round itself is geography as the service world draws it: not squares and terraces but area doors in walking order, each with its own knock, its own temper, and its own standing entry in Nib's unwritten gazetteer. News travels the Walk faster than it travels the wires of the ton's drawing rooms, and arrives more accurate, having been checked at each door against the one form of error the below-stairs world cannot afford, which is getting a neighbour's trouble wrong.

The dairy's proprietress, a vast and placid personage known to three streets simply as Mother, keeps the board, feeds the link-boys on tick that is never collected, and answers all questions about the morning chalk with the same serene formula: that the board was blank when she went to bed and instructive when she rose, and that she has better things to watch at four in the morning than a wall, which, as the whole Walk observes, is not a denial either.

entities.title: Lye Lane
entities.content:
Lye Lane runs behind the east terraces of Grimalkin Square, from the dairy at the bottom to the old wall at the top, and it is the Square's working spine: the lane the coal comes down, the washing goes up, the tradescats' barrows travel, and the gentry never see, except very late, cloaked, and confident of being unobserved, a confidence the lane has been quietly correcting for a century.

Its furniture is the below-stairs world's high street. The dairy and its board at the bottom; the butcher at the wall end, with a framed bill in a fair round hand he shows to customers who doubt that beauty and arithmetic can share a page; Soaper's Court opening off the middle, breathing steam on washdays; the dust yard's gate; and Wick's post at the top, where the lamps give out and the link-boys' trade begins. By day the lane is barrows and shouting. After the Square's lamps are done it becomes the dark quarter-mile, and anything that moves in it moves past Wick, which is to say, into the ledger.

The lane's one law is older than the watch and better kept: what comes down the lane is trade, what goes up the lane is trade, and what happens in the lane stays in the lane's own book, which is not for sale, though it has, once or twice in a century, been consulted.

entities.title: Grimalkin Square, from the area steps
entities.content:
There are two Grimalkin Squares, stacked. The one in the prints: plane trees, fountain, sunning wall, the ton at its parliament. And the one below the pavement line: a continuous underground county of kitchens, sculleries, cellars, and areas, running unbroken behind the terraces, where perhaps four times as many cats live as live above, and where the Square's actual day is manufactured, hot water by six, breakfasts by nine, the whole gleaming stage set fresh each morning by a workforce the audience has agreed not to see.

The area steps are the border crossings between the two Squares, and each set has its own character, known to every tradescat on the round: Blackfriars' scrubbed and welcoming, coal cellar full; Nalewood's ancient, worn hollow in the middle, swept twice daily by tradition older than the broom; the Fluffington steps handsome above and anxious below, where the callers are lately more often owed than owing; and the delegation's steps at the north end, spotless, silent, and giving, in the professional opinion of every below-stairs cat who has delivered there, absolutely nothing away, which in the service world is itself a character reference of a particular kind.

The below-stairs Square keeps the above-stairs one alive and asks, in return, exactly one courtesy, rarely granted: to be paid on time. The sheet's standing table of which houses manage it is the most-read column in The Mews, and has done more for wages on the east terrace, the tubs judge, than forty years of asking politely.

entities.title: The east mews of Grimalkin Square
entities.content:
The east mews runs behind the Fluffington side of the Square, a cobbled canyon of stable doors, coach houses, hay lofts, and the small precise societies that live over them: coach cats, grooms' families, the harness-room card school, and the pigeons nobody official will admit to racing. It is the Square's tradesman's face, and its memory: the mews sees every arrival the front steps announce and every departure they do not, and its verdicts, passed along the loft windows in the evening, are the raw stock of half the intelligence in Mayfur, laundered upstairs, as the saying goes, into the mews says.

Its gates are the east terrace's true doors. The Fluffington mews gate in particular has become, these two seasons, a barometer the whole lane reads: which callers come to it instead of the front, at what hours, with what temper; where the dawn specialist enters, paid in coin at the harness-room door; and which departures leave it at night, cloaked, at a working pace, entered in the appropriate book by the appropriate parties, meaning, the mews will say if pressed, none of your business and all of ours.

The mews' code is the lane's code with horses in it: everything seen, everything remembered, nothing volunteered west of the wall. Its highest term of praise is an honest gate, applied to houses whose back-door business would survive the front door's scrutiny, and its oldest joke, told about every great house in turn and lately about one in particular, is that the finest families keep two sets of books, and the mews keeps the third.

entities.title: The Fluffington book-room
entities.content:
The book-room at Fluffington House is a small square chamber off the back stairs, one window on the mews, one lamp, one desk, and the only room in that establishment, the kitchen holds, where the house's two lives meet on paper: the ballroom life the front windows advertise and the ledger life the area door endures. Miss Inkpaw has kept it eleven years, and keeps it the way Corkindale keeps his cellar: cool, exact, and closed.

The room's habits are the house's pulse, read fluently below stairs. In good months the lamp is out by ten. In audit months it burns late, and the kitchen sends up strong tea without being rung for, on the principle that arithmetic after midnight is a form of night nursing. The May of the comet season the lamp burned past midnight nine nights of thirty, a figure the kitchen still cites when the subject of that spring comes up, which, in that house, it does not.

Its small fame beyond the household is the window. Book-room windows on the mews are the below-stairs world's noticeboards, and the Fluffington one has been read for two seasons like weather glass: lamp late, trouble counting; lamp out early, trouble past counting. The mews does not enjoy the reading. The mews reads it anyway. Accounts, the harness-room says, are like chimneys: no smoke is worse.

entities.title: The kitchen at Almeow's
entities.content:
The most exclusive assembly rooms in the kingdom are served by a kitchen the size of a modest parlour, and the below-stairs world regards the fact as the great standing joke on the ton: five hundred cats of the first fashion, dancing above refreshments a coaching inn would blush at, prepared by a staff of three and distributed by ceremony. The badness of Almeow's refreshments is fashionable Mayfur's oldest running complaint, worn smooth as a doorstep, and the kitchen hears every word of it through the hatch, and smiles, and says nothing, because the kitchen knows what the complaint is actually purchasing.

What it purchases, and what the ton has never once asked, is the difference: the patronesses' table allowance, set generations ago at a figure worthy of the rooms, is spent to perhaps a fifth of its weight on the famous thin lemonade and the biscuits of record, and the remainder goes, by a standing order older than any patroness living and renewed by each committee without discussion, to the widows of the institution's servants, the door's, the kitchen's, the chairmen's, paid quarterly, in full, forever. The dry biscuit, the kitchen holds, is the best-spent money in Mayfur, and cats who mock it are mocking a pension they will never be told about.

On ball nights the kitchen's hatch keeps its own list, longer than Mr. Pounce's and open to all comers: staff, chairmen's boys, link-boys, the watch on its round, fed hot and fed first, the verger himself eating standing at the end. Two worlds, one door, the kitchen says, and ours eats better, and the lemonade is not wasted on us either, there being a second jug, behind the flour bin, of a rather different character.

entities.title: The cellars at Brindle's
entities.content:
Below the deep chairs and the wager book, Brindle's descends into Corkindale's kingdom: three levels of arch and bin, candle sconces polished by a century of careful thumbs, the cheese room with its slate shelves and its audited legends, and a quiet so old and so complete that new boot boys are taken down once, early, to learn what the club is actually made of. The cellars hold the port, the records, and the temperature, in that order of official importance and the reverse order of truth.

The cellar book is the below-stairs counterweight to the wager book upstairs, and the wiser members know it. Wagers record what gentlemen predict; the bins record what they did about it afterward, and on certain famous evenings the two books disagree in ways Corkindale declines to reconcile. The staff's working rule for reading the club's soul: watch the brandy in a crisis, the champagne in a triumph, and the port on the nights nobody upstairs is saying anything at all, the port being the club's own language for matters ruled off in black.

The cellars' unofficial offices are the below-stairs world's quietest: pensions from the cheese allowance, a warm corner by the furnace flue with a mattress in it for any club servant too old or too briefly homeless, and the standing right of the kitchen's mousers to the third level, where the work is real and the wages are paid in kind. The committee knows none of this. The committee, Corkindale judges, pays for all of it, and would only be confused by an itemised bill.

entities.title: The Rookery, from inside the wall
entities.content:
West of the wall the Rookery is a shudder. Inside it, it is an economy, a government, and a memory, in ascending order of importance. The yards run the trades, the Beldam's den runs the law, and the memory runs everything else: who fought, who fed whom in the hungry years, which Mayfur houses paid their tradescats late in which decade, and what the crown's gratitude weighed, measured to the ounce, against its bunting.

The war is not history here; it is infrastructure. The sewer campaign was mustered out of these yards, crew by crew, and the cats who came back came back to the same cellars with new silences, and the Rookery built its whole post-war self around not asking. The untouched plate corner, the standing glass in late spring, the memorial window's fourth-year names, these are not customs, they are load-bearing walls, and the one sure way for an outsider to end a conversation east of the wall is to touch one.

What the service world west of the wall knows, and the ton does not, is how much of Mayfur's below-stairs life is Rookery-staffed and Rookery-raised: the porters, the link-boys, half the kitchens' youngest paws, sent west to earn and sending wages east, the wall being, from this side, not a boundary but a membrane, crossed twice daily by everyone who actually carries the Square. The Mews circulates east of the wall same-day, read aloud at the mint scales by whoever the Beldam gestures at, and the sheet's below-stairs tables are checked here with particular attention, the Rookery being the world's leading authority on what the west end owes.

entities.title: Lower Gnawbury, as the round walks it
entities.content:
On the tradescats' rounds Lower Gnawbury is the gentlest stop in Mayfur: a terrace of thin means and immaculate steps where the orders are small, the payment is slow and certain, and the manners at the area doors are better than at any address twice the size. The terrace's economies are conducted with a discipline the round respects too much to notice aloud: the butcher's boy has standing instructions to mis-weigh in the customer's favour at number four and lose the difference in the book, and the coal cat forgets, every hard January, to collect at two particular doors, a forgetfulness his master audits annually and renews.

Number four is the round's collective ward. The Grey house takes little and is owed much, by an arrangement no single tradesman devised and all of them keep; the good days come up the terrace with the milk, in Nib's particular cry, and on the bad ones the whole round adjusts its noise by unspoken treaty, barrows walked not wheeled, the knife-grinder's wheel silent past the parlour window.

The week in April the house went dark, the round kept its own vigil in its own way: deliveries left without knocking, bills left unwritten, and the apothecary's runner passed through at all hours on a flat run, asked nothing by anybody. The terrace's ruling at the pump afterward stands as the round's official memory of that week, and its whole text: the ending arrived, the particulars are not owed, there is soup to carry.

entities.title: Billingsgate, before the gentry wake
entities.content:
Billingsgate's true day is over before Mayfur's begins, which is why the two have never met. From the last of the dark the market is the loudest, coldest, most exactly honest place in the kingdom: the tide's catch weighed under Sweep's rules on Sweep's half and under older, damper rules on the other, prices called that will govern every kitchen's dinner by noon, and a floor population of stall crews, porters, runners, and gulls conducting the day's first and frankest exchange of news in Town.

For the below-stairs world the market is the morning's second parliament, senior to the tubs and junior only to the scales. Kitchen cats from every quarter meet at the stalls, and what is said over the ice travels home with the fish: the market knew the Fluffington credit was cooked two seasons before Brindle's did, prices being the one witness that cannot be charmed, and it knows to the week which great houses have quietly moved from turbot to whiting while the front windows go on blazing.

The brass plate at the river stairs, the number and no names, is the market's one solemnity. Porters touch it going past on the war's anniversaries; the stalls' first fish of that morning goes east of the wall free, by a custom nobody instituted and nobody would dare end; and Captain Bootes, when his ship is in, comes down at dawn once a season and stands at the plate for a while with his hat off, and buys herring he plainly does not want from whichever stall is nearest, and the market lets him, and charges him honestly, which is Billingsgate's language for respect.

entities.title: The Captain, as the market rates him
entities.content:
The below-stairs world holds few opinions about the quality's heroes, having audited too many. Captain Bootes it makes an exception for, on evidence. The market's file: he pays on the nail, he knows a fair weight by eye, he addresses porters as men of business, and once a season, ship in, he stands at the brass plate with his hat off and buys unwanted herring for the full price, which Billingsgate has decided is the correct way for the west end to visit.

What earned him the Rookery's actual regard, a currency the ton cannot mint, was the toast at Brindle's, reported below stairs by the club's own staff the same night, word for word, with the room's silence included: the war won in the dark by cats this club would not admit to its kitchen. The old runners' verdict, delivered at the scales, was characteristically exact: that the Captain's health was the first thing the fleet ever sent below the waterline, and that it arrived, which is more than the back-pay did.

The kitchens along his dining routes add the small entries that finish a character below stairs: tips fair and unshowy, no bell rung twice, and a standing habit, noted at four separate houses, of asking the door on his way out whether the mews gate is lit for his own coach cat's sake. The sheet's one-line summary, in the number on the quality's manners: some officers leave the service; the service, in the better cases, declines to leave the officer.

entities.title: The Mews, No. 1: a sheet for the counting class
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

This sheet is for us. It will be chalked when there is matter, copied while the copper heats, and gone by the fish, and it will concern itself with the only news that was ever any use below the pavement: what things cost, what work is owed, and who pays.

In this first number, the spring wage table, east terrace, entered plain. One house pays above the rate and to the hour, and every kitchen on the Walk knows which. Three pay the rate. Two pay the rate in promises, and one of those two has begun paying the promises in smaller promises, and the sheet will return to that house at quarter-day with the table updated and the arrears totalled, because an arrear written down plainly has a way of embarrassing itself into coin.

Also in this number: the fish, honest at Sweep's stalls and creative elsewhere, prices below; the price of a link-boy's coat against a single ballroom candle, arithmetic the reader may finish personally; and notice that the dairy board will carry, henceforth, the standing list of houses that charge their girls for candle ends, until the practice stops, which, gentle kitchens, it now will.

You ask who I am. Ask instead why the tradesman's entrance sees everything and is never once looked at. I am the entrance. Doors are the honest half of every house, and it is time the honest half kept a page.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the affair, as the kitchens remember it
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

A year today since the Papers upstairs printed the arithmetic of a certain lordship's courting, and the anniversary being general knowledge above stairs and better knowledge below, the sheet will enter, for the record, the version the kitchens carried through it.

Below stairs knew, of course. A house that is courting orders differently: the flowers double, the good candles come out, the cellar breathes. A house courting twice orders confusingly, and by the second week of it there was not a kitchen on the east terrace that had not done the sums over the teapot. What below stairs did with the knowing was what below stairs does, which is nothing: we are not paid to correct the gentry's hearts, and the two young ladies had mothers, and mothers generally serve the dish in season. That the dish arrived instead by print, dated and worded, was as sharp a surprise at the area door as at the front one, whatever the wagers at Brindle's assumed about servants and secrets, and the sheet notes, with a professional's respect, that in a full year the source of that item has not surfaced in a single kitchen, tap-room, or tub, which for this town is not discretion, it is a miracle of the first water.

The cost below stairs is entered too, because above stairs never counts it. Two blameless households questioned to the pantry shelves, her Grace's inquiry twice through the servants' hall, courteous and endless, the minutes of it taken down as ever by the book-room in that even hand while the questions went round the table. No place lost, which the sheet enters to her Grace's credit. A winter's peace lost in every basement on the east side, which the sheet enters to the account of whoever fed the item upstairs, and the sheet observes only this of them: that they knew what they knew exactly, and what that is worth depends entirely on what it cost them, and the sheet has learned, in a year of keeping this page, that nothing exact is free.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: on the biscuits of record
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The west end's oldest joke is the refreshments at a certain assembly rooms, and on Wednesday last a young gentleman of fashion was heard to declare, at the hatch itself, that the lemonade was an insult to his subscription. The sheet has decided the joke is old enough to retire, and will retire it with arithmetic, gently, and no further than this: the table allowance of that institution, set by its foundresses at a figure worthy of the rooms, is spent to about a fifth of its weight on the famous biscuit, and the difference, gentle kitchens, is spent, quarterly, in full, exactly where you would spend it, and has been for longer than any patroness now living can say, and the sheet declines to embarrass either the biscuit or the board by itemising a farthing further.

The young gentleman may keep his joke. The sheet suggests only that he make it more quietly at the hatch, where the staff eat after him, hot, first, and without complaint, by an arrangement of the door's own keeping that is also nobody's business, and also entered here, initials only, P., with the sheet's compliments.

Prices this week: whiting up a penny on the late tides, candles steady, lye dear again and the court advises buying short. And the east terrace arrears table, updated: one house has cleared to March, which the sheet enters with pleasure, pleasure being rarer on that page than coin.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the specialist's wages
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The sheet prints movements, not meanings, and this week's movements are these.

A certain grooming specialist, an outside cat, no house's servant, attends a certain gate on the east terrace at dawn, daily, and has for above two years. He is paid weekly, in coin, at the harness-room door, and the coin, say cats who have handled its like, has come west over the wall, which coin does more often than the west supposes and minds less than it says. The specialist's wage for one week, the sheet has it exactly, would pay a scullery girl for a quarter. The mews knows his employer's name and the sheet does not print what the mews knows on that subject, the friendly chapter of certain arrangements being, in the sheet's experience, the safest chapter to be quiet in.

Separately, and the sheet does mean separately, cloakroom attendants at two addresses this season report a sweetness in certain gentlemen's evening coats that never came off Ribbon Row, crushed and green at the edges, familiar to any cat who has walked the wall's east side with a working nose. The attendants report it because attendants notice everything and are asked nothing, which is the below-stairs condition entire, and the sheet enters it because the sheet is where what we notice goes.

Two movements, gentle kitchens, entered on one page because they arrived in one week. The sheet does not do meanings. The sheet observes only that coin and sweetness are both travelling the same direction lately, west over the wall and up the back stairs, and that when the traffic reverses, as traffic does, it will be the front stairs that feel it, front stairs being, in the sheet's long observation, the last to hear and the loudest to complain.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the count, as it stood Thursday
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The committee at the assembly rooms sat last evening on the candidacy the whole town has opinions about and the whole wall has one opinion about, and the sheet has the count as it stood when the fires were raked: four against, three for. The sheet's sources are the sheet's sources, but the reader may note that a committee room's tea tray goes up with seven cups and comes down with seven saucers readable as any minute-book, and that the room's fire was laid, tended, and raked by somebody, and somebody generally has ears.

Entered plainly, then, as the count stood at the raking: the candidate declined by four voices to three. The sheet adds the below-stairs particulars the west end's version will not carry. That the candidate has not attended one sitting, being occupied at the scales from four each morning. That his ledgers, which the proposing patroness laid before the committee, were examined by cats who could not themselves survive the examining. And that the kitchen at the rooms, which has fed every committee for forty years and heard every deliberation through the hatch whether it wished to or not, reports this one the longest of its records, and the quietest, and the only one at which a patroness was heard to say that she would want the war explained to her again, slowly, before she voted the wall higher than it stood in it.

The count is the count, gentle kitchens, and the sheet prints counts. It observes only that Thursday's count is Thursday's, and that the tea tray is ordered again for tomorrow, which committees that have finished their business do not generally require.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the count, corrected, and gladly
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The sheet printed yesterday the committee's count as it stood at Thursday's raking, four against, three for, and the sheet stands by its raking. It reports today, with a pleasure it will not pretend to hide, that the count no longer stands. The committee was resummoned Friday, at whose instance the west end may guess and the sheet may not print, and the candidacy was carried, five voices to two. The count changed; so did two minds; and the kitchens knew before the members, the tea tray having gone up Friday with a bottle on it, which in forty years of that committee it never has before.

What was said in the room Friday the sheet does not have and will not invent. What the below-stairs particulars say is this: two carriages at a certain north-terrace door before eleven Friday morning, both patronesses' liveries, both visits short; and the proposing patroness at her own table Friday evening in remarkable appetite, remarking to her reader, who is not the sheet's source, that the room had only wanted the question put where it could not look away from it.

And the candidate. The sheet's correspondent at the morning weigh-in reports that the Governor, informed at his scales that the first rooms in Mayfur had opened to him, weighed out three stone of herring before replying, and replied that the fish would not weigh themselves, and that he was obliged to the ladies, and that the kitchen door of those rooms had fed his boys for years and the front one could not improve on it. The voucher, the sheet understands, will not be taken up. The wall does not mind, gentle kitchens, and the sheet will say plainly why, once, and then keep the page for prices: the wall never wanted the rooms. The wall wanted the sentence said aloud in them, the one about who defended what, and it has now been said, on the record, in the oldest voice in Mayfur, and the wall has taken delivery of the saying and signed for it, and the door may do as it pleases.

Yesterday's number stands in the file as Thursday's truth. This number is Friday's, and Friday's governs. A ledger that cannot correct itself, gentle kitchens, is not a ledger, it is a monument, and the sheet does not build monuments.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: a young gentleman's amends, entered before the pardon
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The west end has spent a week enjoying the ruin of a young lord who overturned a punt at a Venetian breakfast, drowned eleven tablecloths, and sent a distinguished foreign gentleman's hat to the bottom of the Saucerine, and the sheet has read the west end's verdicts and finds them, as usual, a week behind the facts and the wrong way up. The sheet prints the facts, dated.

Monday: the young lord at the park keepers' lodge at six in the morning, unaccompanied, asking, the keepers report, not for absolution but for a drag-rake. Three afternoons this week he has worked the shallows with the keepers for the hat, found Tuesday, and for the boat-boy's pole, found Wednesday, the keepers having permitted the labour on the grounds that the Saucerine does not clean itself and a volunteer is a volunteer whatever his tailoring. Thursday: the laundress at Soaper's Court paid in full for eleven tablecloths at replacement, not laundering, rates, the difference between which, gentle kitchens, is the difference between an apology and an allowance, and the young lord, the court reports, knew it unprompted. And Friday, the entry the sheet rates above the rest: the boat-boy, whose fault the west end had begun by assuming it was, called on at his own yard, by name, and apologised to, by name, in front of his master, which cost the young lord nothing in coin and more than the tablecloths in the only currency the quality is ever short of.

The west end will pardon him in its own time, by its own instruments, for its own reasons, and will believe the pardon was its idea. The sheet enters merely that the amends were made below the waterline first, where amends are weighed and not perfumed, and that the ledger east of the fountain closed his account Friday, paid to the farthing, with a note in the margin the keepers have licensed the sheet to print: this one will do, when the punting is trained out of him.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the clipping, from the area steps
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The sheet has carried the east terrace's hardest arrears table for two years, and it enters this week's movements with the particular care it keeps for houses at their turning.

Monday last, at the at-home of a square-built family the ton still smells herring on, three notes of a certain silver lordship's paper changed paws twice in a quarter hour: from the father's strongbox to the daughter, before the room, and from the daughter and her long-whiskered ally to the fire, before the same room, forgiven entire, with the words, the footmen agree on them, that the ladies had discussed what his lordship's fourteen generations were worth and had decided to find out what he was worth without them. The room, the staff report, did not recover its conversation for a full ten minutes, which at that address is a century.

Wednesday dawn: the specialist attended the east gate as usual and was met, not by the harness-room, but by his lordship, alone, who paid the week's coin in full, shook the specialist's paw, that is in three witnesses' accounts and the sheet triple-enters what it cannot believe, and closed the gate from the inside. Wednesday afternoon: a barber of the plain sort, off Lye Lane, sent for by name, and the great coat of Mayfur clipped to the honest cat beneath, by his lordship's own instruction, the clippings, the sheet has this from the barber's boy, directed to be given to the birds, who, his lordship is reported to have said, at least build with what they are given.

Thursday, this sheet's own table: the Fluffington arrears, standing since the sheet's first number, cleared.
