Wages to the quarter, tradescats to the bill, the boot boy's back-pay with a shilling on it nobody asked for, and Mrs. Suet's kitchen ordering, for the first time in two years, like a kitchen that expects to see the goods. There is a caller from east of the wall who will find, when next he calls at that gate, an account that no longer answers to doors, there being no cloakroom in Mayfur that requires what the house no longer wears, and the sheet is informed, in the way the sheet is informed of eastern matters, that the account is to be written to experience, the east preferring, in its own proverb, a debtor shorn to a debtor stuffed.

The west end will see him at the season's last ball and will make of the sight whatever it makes. The area steps saw him Wednesday, in the plain light, directing his own clipping with his chin up, and the steps' verdict is entered here ahead of the ballroom's, as this sheet's custom now is: lighter by a coat, gentle kitchens, and heavier by nothing at all.

Swept and locked,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: The Mews: the winter ledger
entities.content:
Gentle kitchens,

The knockers come off the doors this week, the quality scatters to its counties, and below stairs begins the other season, the one with the fires banked low and the wages, in the good houses, paid through. The sheet rules off its first full season and enters the totals.

Wages: the east terrace table ends the season cleaner than it began, two houses cleared entire, one by a turning the sheet has already entered and will not gild. Candle ends: the charging of girls for light is ended at every address on the Walk, the sheet having printed the practice monthly until the practice died of the light. The link-boys: coated, all of them, by a subscription the sheet did not organise and cannot attribute, three deliveries of coal to the porters' lodge last winter having apparently established a fashion, and fashions, gentle kitchens, are the one western export the east has ever found useful.

The season's sentence, for the sheet's money, was said in a committee room on a Friday, in the oldest voice in Mayfur, and signed for at the scales. The season's sight was a silver lordship in the plain light of his own mews, chin up. The season's quietest entry is one the sheet holds over, there being matters below stairs as sealed as any above, and the sheet keeps its seals the same way the great archives do, which is how the reader may trust the pages that are open.

The sheet winters as the kitchens winter: at work, with the fires low. The chalk returns with the knockers. Until then, the standing tables govern, the dairy board keeps the prices, and any kitchen in want this winter knows which doors knock back, ours having been, since the first number, that kind of page.

Swept and locked, and the key under no brick you know of,
THE AREA CAT

entities.title: Private ledger: the book-room file, and the rule it lives under
entities.content:
The anniversary number has me back through the old rounds, an audit habit, and I am entering the book-room file properly, under the rule, so that the file itself remembers why it is thin.

The pattern, across two years of night rounds: Miss I. of the east terrace walks late in audit months. Not often; not far; at a working pace, out and back inside the quarter hour, always when the book-room lamp has burned past midnight, which in that house means the columns are fighting. The May of the comet season the lamp burned nine nights of thirty and she walked twice. A clerk who takes the lane's air at one in the morning when the arithmetic will not sit is a clerk with sense, and the ledger has always entered her walks the way it enters Sergeant Paddock's rounds: as the night working, not the night misbehaving.

The rule, restated for the file's own conscience, because the sheet's whole authority hangs on it: respected staff get the reading their record has purchased. Eleven years, not one repeated confidence, the tweeny's doctor paid off a clerk's wage, a hand the whole service world sets its kittens by. Against that ledger, a midnight errand is a midnight errand. I have watched the quality convict servants on thinner coincidence than I hold on anyone, and the day this page starts doing the drawing rooms' work for them, in the drawing rooms' style, the sheet is just the Town Tabby with soot on.

Entered, ruled, and the file closed to the thickness it has earned, which is this page and no more. The books balance better in the quiet. Let her walk.

entities.title: Private ledger: the printers' canvass, concluded
entities.content:
Two years of asking, entered and closed. Every printing house in Town drinks somewhere, and every devil and boy of the trade has, at one time or another this two years, been stood his half-pint within hearing of the only question the below-stairs world has never answered: who sets the Society Papers.

The result is a clean nothing, and a clean nothing from printers' boys is information of the first weight. Type is a hand like any other; the boys know every house's founts the way Nib knows knockers; and the Papers' type, they agree to a boy, belongs to no house in Town, no jobbing shop, no church-crypt press, no gentleman's toy in a library. Nor does any paper-maker's cart deliver a stock that answers to it, and I have had the carts watched through two seasons for the pleasure of being sure.

Conclusion, filed: the Papers are not printed in Town, or not by any trade that drinks, and both of those sentences are ridiculous, and one of them is true, and the file goes face down with the legends, where ridiculous true things belong. The authoress keeps her press the way the court keeps its wall: nobody's business, everybody's furniture.

One professional note, for this page only. The sheet is chalk and copy-paw, and will stay chalk and copy-paw, whatever it could afford. A sheet with no press has no press to find. I learned that from her, whoever she is, the way one tradesman learns from another across a street neither of them crosses.

entities.title: Private ledger: the other account book, appraised
entities.content:
A professional file on the establishment upstairs, kept because two account books in one town should at least know each other's weights and measures, even if they never share a table.

The appraisal, entered fair. The Society Papers are never wrong. I have checked them for two seasons against the only instruments I own, prices, hours, deliveries, and where our pages overlap they have never once misstated a fact I could weigh. That is not luck and it is not access; that is method, and the method smells like mine: somebody up there keeps things in order, with dates, next to each other, and reads the file before the pen moves. The Papers have also twice printed the mews says, which is this sheet travelling upstairs without its name, and the ledger enters the citation with the dry pride of a tradesman whose work is worn by cats who would not receive him.

The limit, entered just as fair. The Papers have never once been below the pavement. Not wrong about us; silent about us, which above stairs comes to the same thing. They know the ballroom's arithmetic to the farthing and do not know what the ballroom's candles cost the girls who trim them, and the not-knowing is not unkindness, it is architecture: that pen was made in the rooms it writes about, the way this chalk was made in the yards. Two instruments, gentle ledger, each true where it was forged. The town's whole account exists in no single book, and I have begun to suspect it never will, and that the town is fortunate in its bookkeepers anyway, both of them, if the word both may be entered once, in the private pages, without vanity.

On the standing question, the file keeps one deliberately thin page, and the rule from the wash-yard governs it: heard, filed, not tested. The court does not spend its own furniture, and some walls, this trade has taught me, hold more than bricks.

entities.title: The authoress, as below stairs reads her
entities.content:
Below stairs reads the Society Papers the way it reads everything the west end produces: secondhand, next morning, and with its own audit running. The verdict, settled years ago at the tubs and never since revised: the great lady of the type is the one member of the ton who does honest work, and the proof is in the instrument, because her facts weigh true at our scales too, and no cat who was ever wrong about the gentry's dinners could stay right about their debts.

What the service world notices that the ton does not: the Papers' mercies run downhill. The names withheld are, three times in four by the tubs' count, the names of cats who could not have survived the printing, and the full treatment is reserved for cats whose coats would break the fall. Below stairs, which has watched the quality's other instruments for centuries, knows exactly how rare that tuning is, and extends to the unknown authoress the only tribute it pays the west end: it does not try very hard to find out who she is. The question is discussed, of course, at every sink in Mayfur, the way the weather is discussed. It is not pursued. There is a difference, and the difference is respect.

The kitchens' one standing observation, polished smooth as the copper: whoever she is, she was never below stairs a day in her life, because the Papers know every card table in Mayfur and have never once printed what a kitchen knows by Tuesday. The tubs do not hold it against her. A pen is forged where it is forged. But the mornings her sheet and ours agree on a fact, gentle reader of nobody's pages, the town is briefly, completely, and doubly true, and the old laundress used to say those were the mornings the linen came up whitest, and nobody has ever been sure she was joking.

entities.title: Private ledger: the specialist, traced and filed
entities.content:
The full file, of which the sheet printed a fifth, entered before the number runs so the state of knowledge is dated prior, a habit I am told the archives of better houses keep.

The specialist: an outside cat, no house's man, lodging east of the wall over the second fence yard, walks west before dawn six days in seven, two hours at the east terrace gate, walks home by the wall's north gap. The wage: weekly, in coin, at the harness-room door, counted twice by the paying paw, which is not the house's habit with any other tradesman and tells the ledger the coin does not begin its journey in that house. The coin itself: handled twice on its way through the lane's ordinary trades, and cats whose paws know the east's coin from the west's, and there are such paws on this lane, say it is east's, and recent, and not lonely.

The employer of record: none. The employer of fact: the file has the name the mews has, the one-eared interest, taken from the lodging, the fence yard, and the company the specialist keeps on quarter-nights, and the file holds the name and the sheet will not print it, the friendly chapter being what it is. What the interest buys for its coin is a coat's daily glory, and what a coat's glory secures, the ledger does not speculate, speculation being the wager book's trade. The ledger notes only the shape: the east pays west, daily, for the upkeep of the west's most admired object, and nothing east of the wall has ever yet been paid for admiration.

Cross-entry, the cloakroom sweetness: three addresses now, dates filed, always ball nights, always the same few coats, and the attendants' noses do not err, noses below stairs being working instruments. The two files sit in the same drawer. The drawer is not a conclusion. The drawer is a drawer, and spring will open it or the east will, and the ledger can wait; the ledger is the one party in Mayfur that is never in a hurry, hurry being how the quality misses things.

entities.title: Private ledger: the April week, entered and left folded
entities.content:
Entered late, deliberately, after the terrace's ruling at the pump, and under it.

The week the Grey house went dark: six nights, no lights, the round's vigil kept the way the round keeps vigils, deliveries without knocking, bills unwritten. Jessop on flat runs at all hours, twice at midnight from the plain end of Ribbon Row, and a large gentleman waiting both midnights at the physician's mews, no name given, none needed on this side of the pavement, paying the after-hours rate without counting it. The seventh morning Nib's cry came up the terrace again, and the terrace, the ledger is reliably told, heard it from behind its doors before the cans were down, every house awake early, nobody willing to be seen waiting.

The fortnight after: accounts that had gathered dust for a year settled across four trades, quietly, in coin, the sums not small and the paying paw not hiding, exactly, but not lingering either. The ledger enters the sequence because the ledger enters sequences; it is what a ledger is for.

The same week, for completeness, since the two files will be read side by side by anyone who ever inherits this drawer: the west end spent those days enjoying a wonder of its own, a great house's treasure abroad without leave, the wager book pricing a certain ringed tail by the hour. The mews' own entry on that subject is one line and closes the page: the same week the west end priced the tail, the east end watched it wait in a physician's mews at midnight, twice, and of the two employments the ledger knows which one it believes in, and the arithmetic between them is nobody's arithmetic below this pavement, the pump having ruled the particulars not owed. The ending arrived. There was soup to carry. Folded, and filed, and the drawer shut on it.

entities.title: Private ledger: Thursday night, the committee room read from below
entities.content:
Entered on the night, fire still warm in the grate below the committee room's, for the number that will chalk before dawn.

The sitting: two hours and the quarter. The tray: seven cups up, seven saucers down, two cups barely touched, and the kitchen has sat enough committees to read a cold cup, a cold cup being a patroness talking. The fire: raked at the half hour past ten, and the raking cat, who has laid that grate for eleven years and is nobody's fool and nobody's source but mine, brought down three particulars with the ash pan. That the count went four against, three for, on the second putting. That the room was quieter than any blackball sitting in its memory, no triumph in the four, which the kitchen enters as the evening's true news, shame being a slower vote than pride. And that one of the seven, which one the grate could not see, said, late, into a silence, that she would want the war explained to her again, slowly, before she voted the wall higher than it stood in it, and that nobody answered her, and the sitting ended not long after.

The tray is ordered again for tomorrow. Committees that have finished do not order trays. The kitchen's book says the question is still breathing, and the kitchen's book on that room has not been wrong in the eleven years the grate has had its present keeper.

The count chalks as it stood, because the sheet prints the raking, not the hope. But the ledger enters the hope too, on this page, where hopes are allowed: that the second tray finds the seventh cup warm.

entities.title: The young lord, as the keepers' ledger has him
entities.content:
Until this July the below-stairs file on young Lord Frisk was one line long and affectionate enough: energy in want of a foreman. The lane's youngest trades liked him on the simple evidence that he greets link-boys by looking at them, a habit so rare in his class that Wick once followed him half a street out of professional disbelief.

The Venetian breakfast lengthened the file. The punt, the eleven tablecloths, the foreign gentleman's hat: the west end had its week of theatre over the wreckage. The keepers' ledger at the Saucerine, which is the below-stairs record of that water, has the sequel the theatre missed: six mornings, one drag-rake, a hat recovered, a boat-boy's pole recovered, replacement rates paid at the court without being asked twice, and an apology delivered by name, in the boy's own yard, in front of the boy's own master, which is the only venue where an apology to a working boy counts and the only one the quality never thinks of.

The keepers' margin note has been licensed to the sheet and framed at the lodge, and the file adopts it as the standing verdict: this one will do, when the punting is trained out of him. Below stairs does not pardon, pardoning being the west end's ceremony; below stairs re-prices, and the young lord's price east of the fountain is good, gentle ledger, and rising, and the Ambassador's household, asked at their own area door, report his Excellency kept the recovered hat wet side out for a week, for the pleasure of telling the story, which the file enters as the season's one diplomatic triumph nobody had to smooth over.

entities.title: Private ledger: the winter handoff, for the spring keeper of this drawer
entities.content:
The chalk sleeps with the knockers. The ledger does not sleep, but it thins, winter below stairs being work without events, and before it thins I am ruling the spring page now, for the cat I will be when the wall warms, in the manner I am told the best archives keep: the open matters, in order of weight, so that spring inherits a desk and not a drift.

One: the sweetness file. The specialist's chapter closed with the clipping, and the east wrote its account to experience, but the cloakroom list was still growing at season's end, three addresses, same few coats, and a trade that has lost its footman does not retire, it re-hires. Watch the new season's first ball nights; watch the cloakrooms; the mint will send a new carrier up the back stairs by May, and the ledger wants his gait on file before the west end smells anything.

Two: the wage tables reopen at Lady Day, and the two houses that cleared must stay cleared; the sheet's authority is that its tables never forget, so the tables must never forget.

Three: the legend audit, unfinished. The court's stock of stories has three entries still unweighed, and the ledger's rule stands, heard, filed, not tested, but an audit half done is a door half shut, and I dislike the draught.

Four, entered last because it weighs most and files thinnest: the other account book. Two seasons now the town has been kept by two pages, each true where it was forged, and this season, for the first time, each page knows the other is being kept. Nothing has passed between us and nothing will, that is not how lighthouses work. But the spring keeper of this drawer should know what the winter one concluded, watching the Papers rule off their season two days before ours: that the town's whole truth is now a thing that exists, gentle ledger, for the first time in its history. It is merely kept in two places, and the two places are not on visiting terms, and whoever finds the way to read both books in one sitting will know Mayfur better than Mayfur has ever known itself. The ledger does not expect to meet such a reader. The ledger keeps its page fit to be read by one, which is the whole discipline of this trade, and the old laundress's mornings can do the rest.

Swept, locked, and the fires banked. Until the wall warms.

entities.title: The Servants' Ball
entities.content:
Once a year, on the night the quality departs for the country and the knockers come off the doors, the service world holds the only ball in Mayfur where the dancing is voluntary. The Servants' Ball has no fixed address, that being the point: it moves each year to whichever great house's staff won the drawing at the last one, the family being safely gone, the covers on the furniture, and the below-stairs of a dozen establishments arriving through the mews like a tide coming home.

Its protocols are the ton's, inverted with precision and love. The precedence is by service, not birth: the longest-serving cat in the room opens the dancing, which last year was the Nalewood butler at forty years and a waltz nobody present will forget. The refreshments are magnificent, every kitchen bringing its actual best, the dishes the quality never taste because they are made from skill rather than expense. And the toast of the evening never varies: to absent friends, drunk standing, in a silence that holds the war, the hungry years, and every cat who served a house that never learned their name.

What is said at the ball stays at the ball, a law older than the sheet and better kept than most of the crown's. The Mews attends, presumably, and has never once printed a word from inside, which below stairs takes as the finest proof of the sheet's character it owns. The one standing exception is the reading: each year, by custom now, somebody reads the seven verses about the brother who goes out at night, and each year it is somebody different, because each year the cat who read last time declines, on the grounds of once being enough.

entities.title: The war, as the service world carried it
entities.content:
The histories say the war against the Rat King was won by the fleet, the militias, and at the last the sewer runners, and the histories are right, and below stairs adds the ledger the histories never open: every crew of runners was fed from somebody's kitchen, guided by somebody's link-boys, and nursed, the ones who came up, in somebody's scullery, because the hospitals of Mayfur did not take cats without addresses and the basements of Mayfur did.

The service world's war was logistics. Kitchens on half rations sent bread east; the Milk Walk ran messages under the cans when the crown's own riders would not cross the wall after dark; the laundries boiled bandages by night and table linen by day and never once confused the accounts. And when it ended, the same basements watched the bunting go up for the fleet and took their own veterans back down the area steps without a word, because the war below stairs ended the way everything below stairs ends: with the fires to be laid in the morning.

The habits that survive are quiet and absolute. The untouched corner of the plate, kept east of the wall and in more western kitchens than the west suspects. The standing rule at Billingsgate that the anniversary's first fish goes east free. The memorial window at St. Gertrude's, whose fourth-year names the service world reads aloud to its kittens, one by one, because the Reverend fought four years to get them carved and the least the living can do is pronounce them. The sheet prints nothing on the anniversary itself. The sheet's founder ruled, in an early private page, that some ledgers are kept by the parties themselves, and audited nowhere.

entities.title: The hungry years
entities.content:
Between the war's end and the first good harvests, Mayfur below the pavement starved politely for three winters, and the shape of the present Rookery was cast in that cold. The crown's back-pay never came; the granaries were rebuilding; and the west end, which had danced the victory, discovered a fatigue of the subject that below stairs has neither forgotten nor much mentioned, mentioning being a currency the poor spend carefully.

What happened instead of help was organisation. The Beldam's first catmint garden dates from those winters, grown, she has said, because the veterans needed somewhere soft to put the dark, and the judgment of what the trade later became belongs to later. Sweep's first stall dates from them, bought with pit winnings and run at cost through two Februaries, the profit line in his oldest ledger reading, in a young cat's careful hand, not this year. Sergeant Paddock's occurrence book developed its famous inability to spell during them. And the arrangement the service world still lives by, that the last hour's catch goes east at cost, that the dairy feeds link-boys on tick it never collects, that no kitchen lets a known child go hungry two doors from its own fire, all of it is hungry-years law, kept now the way all real law is kept: as habit, by cats who no longer remember it was ever invented.

The sheet has printed the era exactly once, in the number on unthanked offices, as a single line of arithmetic: what the war cost the yards in cats, against what the peace paid them in pensions, the second figure being a zero the type-setter was instructed to make no smaller than the first.

entities.title: The candle-ends campaign
entities.content:
The sheet's first sustained campaign, and its proof of concept. The practice: certain houses charged their youngest maids for the candle ends the girls read by, docking the wage for light the house had already burned once. It was old, it was petty, it was perfectly legal, and it had survived every polite objection ever raised against it, politeness being a weapon the practice's beneficiaries owned outright.

The Mews did not object. The Mews published a table. House by house, month by month, the standing list of establishments that charged their girls for light, updated with the milk, without adjectives, the sheet's whole editorial line being one sentence at the column's head: the following houses find this fair. The first month, two houses came off the list with statements of clarification the sheet printed without comment. The third month, a patroness was overheard at Almeow's asking her neighbour whether her own house was on it, not being entirely sure, and by the fifth the list was blank and the sheet retired it with the only flourish it has ever permitted itself: a single line of type reading, this table is discontinued for want of entries.

Below stairs dates its respect for the sheet from that campaign, and above stairs never knew it happened, which the tubs consider the most elegant part. The campaign's method became the sheet's method entire: no accusations, no meanings, just the fact, printed plainly, at intervals, until the fact got embarrassed and left town.

entities.title: The standing order behind the biscuit
entities.content:
The oldest kind secret in Mayfur is written in a minute-book nobody reads, in the hand of a patroness four generations dead: the standing order that governs the table allowance of the first assembly rooms in the kingdom. The order's operative sentence has been renewed by every committee since without discussion, largely because no committee has ever thought to look up what it actually spends, the badness of the refreshments being assumed to be a tradition rather than a transaction.

Below stairs knows the transaction to the farthing, because below stairs administers it. A fifth of the allowance buys the lemonade and the biscuit of record. The remainder is paid out quarterly, by the kitchen, on the door's accounting, to the widows of the institution's own service: the door's, the kitchen's, the chairmen's, the musicians', in full, forever, under a heading in the institution's books so dull that no auditor has ever read past its title. Three patronesses in living memory have discovered it, each by accident, and each, after one conversation at the hatch, has renewed the order and declined the credit, which the kitchen holds is the order working exactly as designed: a kindness built to survive its own discovery.

The sheet printed the arithmetic once, gently, without the destination, and considers the matter permanently closed. Some funds are guarded best by a dry biscuit and a joke the whole town tells in the wrong direction.

entities.title: Mother, of the Milk Walk dairy
entities.content:
Nobody now working the Walk remembers the dairy before Mother, and the institution has arranged its beliefs accordingly: she is held to have come with the building, like the pump. A vast, placid, cream-and-grey presence of no stated age, she runs the dawn yard with a stillness that organises everything around it, prices called once, cans counted by ear, disputes settled by the simple expedient of Mother looking at the parties until one of them remembers an errand.

Her ledger of standing kindnesses is the Walk's constitution. The link-boys eat at the yard on tick that has never once been collected in anyone's memory, an arrears Mother carries forward each year under a heading she declines to explain. The third scullery girls of six houses take their tea at her bench on their half-days, where nobody asks them to fetch anything. And any cat newly turned off without a character knows, because the whole Walk knows, that the dairy needs a paw for a week or two exactly as often as somebody needs a week or two, the vacancy appearing and closing with the need, never advertised, never named.

On the board and its morning chalk she maintains her one policy: blank when she sleeps, instructive when she rises, and better things to watch at four than a wall. On the question that follows from it she has been asked, over the years, in every register from sly to direct, and has answered every version the same way: by topping up the asker's can a splash past the measure, which the Walk has decided means either nothing or everything, and has stopped deciding which.

entities.title: The flies crew at the Theatre Royal
entities.content:
Above the five gilt tiers, up where the chandelier's chains anchor and the scenery hangs like weather waiting to happen, the Theatre Royal belongs to the flies crew: four cats and a foreman who move the sky for a living and watch, from the best seats in the house, everything the house believes is private. The crew is Rookery to a cat, recruited for head and nerve, and holds the fly floor by a tenure older than the management, no performance having ever once been stopped by anything the crew could reach in time.

What the flies see is the theatre's true second show. The boxes conduct their season under the crew's feet: the notes passed, the hands held below the sill line, the visitors who arrive during the dark scenes and leave before the lights. The crew's code on all of it is the lane's code at altitude, everything seen, nothing sold, and its one exception is carved into crew law by the case that made it: information moves, free and fast, when somebody below is about to be hurt. It was the flies who got word east the night the card-ring tried to settle a debt in the gallery stairwell, and the debt's collectors discovered, descending, that the stairwell had unaccountably filled with stagehands.

The sheet and the flies deal in weather reports: the crew confirms prices and hours like anyone else, and on the rest maintains that what happens above the chandelier stays above the chandelier. The gallery cats, the humbler observers who watch from the cheap height, are a different institution with different rules, and the two do not poach, the air rights of the Theatre Royal having been settled by treaty longer ago than anyone can date.

entities.title: The fly floor at the Theatre Royal
entities.content:
The fly floor runs the width of the Theatre Royal above the proscenium, a timber gallery of cleats, ropes, and counterweights where the scenery lives between its entrances and the crew lives between everything. It is reached by a ladder the management has never climbed, lit by what leaks up from the chandelier, and floored with boards whose gaps provide, entirely incidentally, the most complete view of the house that exists: every box, every tier, the pit, the stage, and the gallery, all at once, from directly above.

The floor's furniture is functional and storied: the counterweight bench where the crew takes its suppers, the rope locker that has held, at various times, a fugitive, a wedding breakfast, and the Ambassador's recovered hat overnight for safekeeping; and the foreman's slate, on which the night's cues are chalked and rubbed out, and which has, in forty years, never once carried anything else, the crew holding that a slate with opinions on it is a slate that gets somebody dropped.

Below stairs rates the fly floor the best post in Mayfur for a young cat with a head for heights and a mouth that shuts: the wages are theatre wages, poor, but the education is total, and the crew's alumni are scattered through the service world in positions where seeing everything and saying nothing turned out, to nobody's surprise, to be the entire qualification.

entities.title: La Gattina, as the chorus banks her
entities.content:
The house sees the diva: the cancellations, the feuds, the upper register that has cracked two chandelier pendants and one engagement. The dressing-room corridor sees the other account, and the chorus, who are paid least and know most, keep it with the fierceness of cats defending a kindness they cannot afford to lose. La Gattina feeds them. Not grandly, constantly: the pot in her dressing room on performance nights is for the corridor, filled by her own dresser on her own coin, and a chorus cat sung hoarse or gone hungry answers to her personally, management being, in her stated view, a species of weather one does not consult about soup.

Her cancellations, the corridor will tell you if it trusts you, run on a private meteorology: she cancels when the voice is at risk, and the voice is the chorus's roof as well as hers, a season of La Gattina in ruin being a season of empty houses and shorter wages. The temperament is real, the corridor concedes, and also load-bearing: a diva who may erupt is a diva nobody overworks, and the protection extends, like her pot, corridor-wide.

On the standing question of the other papers, the corridor's testimony is dry: the great lady upstairs is always a week behind on the opera, which the dressing rooms find eternally funny, the opera being the one house in Mayfur where the private life happens in public and the performances are the discreet part. The sheet, for its part, prints her prices, her benefit nights, and nothing else, and received, after the wet Thursday, a note in a soprano's sprawling hand containing a single sentence in the southern tongue, which the sheet had translated, framed, and has declined to explain to anybody.

entities.title: The standing wage tables
entities.content:
The sheet's wage tables are four columns of type that changed the east terrace more than any sermon, statute, or scandal of the age: house, rate, punctuality, arrears, published with the milk at every quarter-day and updated between when movement warrants. They are compiled from the only sources that cannot be charmed, the paid and the unpaid themselves, cross-checked at the tubs, the stalls, and the area doors, and they have never once been successfully disputed, two attempts having ended with the disputing house's own books proving the sheet's figure to the shilling.

Their power is architectural. A house's table entry is read by every cat who might take a place there, every tradescat who might extend it credit, and every below-stairs parent weighing a first position for a kitten, which means the tables converted wages from a private mercy into a public price, and prices, as the sheet observed in an early number, are the one form of gossip the gentry respect. The two houses that cleared their arrears this season did not do it because kindness broke out. They did it because the table does not forget, and the sheet's authority rests on the tables the way the tables rest on the tubs: all the way down, on cats who count.

The original compilation, the first season's master sheet in the Area Cat's own chalk-then-copy hand, is held, the Walk believes, wherever the ledgers are held, which is to say: nobody knows, and the not-knowing is considered part of the furniture.

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 17: The Season Opens
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

We are returned. The knockers are back on the doors, the sunning wall has resumed its parliament, and the Dowager Countess of N. wore the collar to the opening ball, seventeen pearls and three centuries, and the season, as is constitutionally required, thereby began.

The early intelligence. The ward of a certain black-and-white Grace has returned from the country with her ribbon, her eyes, and, this authoress suspects, a plan of campaign that would impress a field marshal; the incumbent diamond has returned with her voice and her records intact; and the two are to share a Town of finite ballrooms, which is the best news this paper has had in a twelvemonth.

Also returned: a certain ginger gentleman, seen at Billingsgate before dawn shaking paws east of the wall. Also not returned: the money of a certain silver lordship, though the coat, remarkably, persists in its glory. And at Almeow's, the patronesses convene Thursday on the gravest question ever put to them, of which this paper will say only: the candidate has cleaner ledgers than his judges, and the Dowager knows it, and so, now, do you.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 19: On a Locked Room
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The Nalewood Collar is gone. I print it plainly because the whispered versions are already worse, and because the facts deserve better handling than they are getting at Brindle's, where a book was opened before the Dowager's household had finished breakfast, which even for that institution is brisk.

The facts: a locked case, a locked room, a house never robbed in living memory, and no mark on any of it. Two witnesses place a large gentleman with a ringed tail in the mews, and the wagering has done its arithmetic aloud. This authoress will do hers in silence, and offers the book's subscribers three observations gratis. First: the gentleman in question has never in his career taken anything whose loss would grieve a cat he respects, and his respects, though eccentrically distributed, are known. Second: the house was not entered by any means its locks were built to argue with, and there are perhaps three sets of paws in Town with that particular education, and one of them is dead. Third: the Dowager has declined the runners, declined the reward, and is, my sources agree, not in the least alarmed.

A lady who has lost three centuries of pearls does not decline help, gentle reader. Unless the pearls are not lost.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 20: The Collar Comes Home
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The collar is home. Eleven nights abroad, returned as it went, through locks that did not notice, into a case that never learned it had been empty, and beside it, my sources are unanimous, a sprig of dried heather, which cats of the Highlands will tell you is an apology, and cats of longer memory will tell you is a receipt.

Brindle's wishes to know who. This authoress finds herself occupied by a better question: why does a cat who can walk through the oldest locks in Mayfur take a treasure he then returns? Not for profit; the collar never reached a fence, and I would know. Not for spite; the heather forbids it. Which leaves need, gentle reader: eleven days of need, somewhere, that seventeen pearls and three centuries could answer, and then come home.

The Dowager has closed the matter, and this paper, which closes nothing, will on this occasion honour the decree, for its own reasons. I will note only what she said at her table, since it deserves the permanence of type: the collar has been somewhere it was needed, and it is home now, and we will speak of the weather.

We will speak of the weather, gentle reader. But I will keep the receipt.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 22: In Praise of a Needle
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A short number this week, Town having behaved itself, an outrage I trust will not be repeated.

Let us therefore praise Madame Sphynx. The ton brings that lady its bodies and its secrets in the same hour, and she fits the one and files the other, and in ten years on Ribbon Row not a single confidence has left her atelier by any door this authoress watches, and I watch them all. Asked again this season whether she is myself, Madame replied that a modiste who printed what she heard would lose her clients, and thereby her hearing, and what kind of fool dismantles her own loom. It is the most sensible thing said in Mayfur this year, and I commend it to the gentlemen of Brindle's, who have never once asked what Lady Whiskerdown stands to lose, and might learn something from the arithmetic.

Also this week: young Lord F. has been readmitted to the Theatre Royal on his solemn oath regarding the chandelier, which the management has accepted, and insured against.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 24: On Bridges
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

You will have heard that something occurred at midnight on the Saucerine bridge. You will have heard it because everyone has heard it, and everyone has heard it because a great house has forbidden its discussion, and Town, presented with a locked door, always checks whether the key is under the mat.

This paper knows what occurred. This paper is not going to print it.

I am aware this will disappoint the readers who take my masthead for a promise of total war, and I owe them, if not the item, then the principle withheld with it. Here it is. This authoress prints what the ton does in its ballrooms, because ballrooms are theatres and the tickets are sold. What two cats say to each other alone at midnight, before anything has been decided, while everything is still costing them something, is not yet conduct, gentle reader. It is still choosing. I report the play. I do not report the rehearsal.

Some bridges are for crossing, and some are for deciding not to, and the difference is nobody's business until the crossing. When there is conduct, you will read it here first.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 26: One Wet Thursday
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

This authoress attended the benefit at the Theatre Royal on Thursday with every intention of reporting it in her usual manner, and finds, three drafts later, that the usual manner will not serve. You will forgive a plain account.

The house was full to the gallery. La Gattina sang unpaid and, those who know say, unequalled; the Ambassador wept without the smallest attempt at diplomacy; a young lord subscribed a sum that made his guardian sit down, and gave as his reason a kindness at a party years old, which this paper records so that the gentlemen who laugh at the boy may know what they are laughing at. And in the front box, in his best collar, sat the Honourable P.G., being looked after, for one whole evening, by the entire world at once, and looking, if I may risk my reputation for accuracy, entirely well.

One item more. The first subscription, made publicly, before the committee could open its book, came from a large gentleman whose tail this paper has had occasion to mention in other contexts. The sum raised eyebrows. The gentleman declined all questions. This authoress finds she has none.

Some weeks, gentle reader, the account book of Town shows a profit.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 28: On Borrowed Plumage
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A question of natural history. When a bird is seen in feathers finer than its diet can explain, the naturalist does not admire the feathers. The naturalist asks what the bird has promised, and to whom.

Mayfur has lately acquired some very fine feathers. There is a coat in this Town, gentle reader, you will know it, everyone knows it, that gleams at a cost its owner's visible fortune stopped explaining two years ago. There is a smell in certain cloakrooms this season that does not come off Ribbon Row: crushed and green, sweet at the edges, familiar to any cat who has walked east of the wall with their nose working. And there is, my sources in that direction assure me, a ledger east of the wall in which certain western names now appear, at interest no bank would print, secured against things no bank would take.

I have pulled this thread twice before in these pages and been patient. I am informed, by parties who ought to know, that the parties who ought to worry know I am pulling it. Good. Let this number stand as my card, formally left: this authoress is at home to the question of the coat, and will receive.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 30: The State of the Diamond
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Midsummer, and the diamond question stands where the wager book has it: even, and getting expensive.

An appreciation of the combatants, since we are privileged to watch them. Her Highness fights as the great bloodlines fight, by existing very beautifully in the correct location; her leap remains the finest thing at Almeow's and her contempt for the contest is itself a weapon, since nothing argues rank like refusing to defend it. The challenger fights as farms fight: early, daily, and for the warm spot. Her retreat at the musicale is already taught, I am told, by governesses. Her management of a certain ducal guardian is the finest sustained performance in Town, and the knot of her ribbon has become a language, which this paper is compiling into a grammar.

The patronesses could settle it and have discovered they prefer the theatre. This authoress declines to tip her own book, but offers the wall this much: bloodline is what you are given, gentle reader, and campaign is what you do, and Town has always said it honours the first while betting, quietly, on the second. The autumn will tell us which it believes.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 31: On Double Entry
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

A short lesson in bookkeeping, the season being briefly becalmed. Single entry records what happened. Double entry records what it cost, and to whom, and any honest house, the accountants insist, requires both columns or it is not keeping books, it is keeping stories.

This authoress has been informed, by channels she declines to describe even to herself, that Mayfur has lately become an honest house: that somewhere below the level at which Town conducts its self-regard, a second account book is being kept, in another hand, concerning itself with the column this paper was never positioned to enter: what the season costs, and to whom, at the prices actually paid. I have not seen it. I am reliably assured I could not obtain it, which is the most promising thing I have heard about any publication in years.

Professional courtesy, then, extended across a distance this paper will not pretend to measure: Town is at last in double entry, gentle reader, and the audit will be the better for it. You have spent seven years asking who I am. I permit myself one season of enjoying that somewhere below your breakfast rooms, somebody may now be asking it about somebody else.

Also this week: a certain punt remains at the bottom of the Saucerine, its late occupant does not, and the paper will attend to that arithmetic when the sum is complete. It is not complete.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 32: The Venetian Breakfast
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The Frostwhisker Venetian breakfast will be remembered as the season's finest entertainment by everyone except its hostess, its caterers, and the eleven tablecloths now at rest in a laundry the ton could not find with a map. The facts, in the order the water received them: one punt, overloaded by exactly one young lord; one fountain-side table, taken broadside; one ambassadorial hat, last seen navigating toward the carp with what witnesses describe as genuine diplomatic composure.

His Excellency laughed until assisted to a chair, which Town has decided settles the matter of offence. The matter of everything else has been referred, as such matters are, to the boy's guardian, and the guardian's face at the moment of referral has been described to this authoress by three witnesses, each of whom required a restorative afterward. The young lord is to the country, rusticated until further notice, and the ton has entered its verdict with the speed it reserves for the friendless and the nineteen: ruined, they say, for the season at least, possibly for the reign.

This paper declines to co-sign the verdict, and will say only why, in the form of a question it invites the wagering interest to sit with: what a cat overturns matters less, gentle reader, than what he rights afterward, and the season is long, and the paper's book on this particular entry remains, pointedly, open.

Also this week, and gravely: the patronesses sit Thursday on the question this paper flagged at the season's opening. The candidate's ledgers have not blushed. It remains to be seen whether the committee's can say the same. The paper will report what the room decides. The paper already knows what the war decided, and so, gentle reader, do you.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 33: What Was Said in the Room
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

You will have heard that the committee voted Thursday, and how it stood, and that it was made to sit again Friday, and how it stands now: carried, five to two, and the walls of King Street still standing, to the visible surprise of two of the five.

What turned it, since Town has invented six versions and will not like losing them: no speech. The Dowager Countess of Nalewood does not make speeches twice, and her first, delivered without notes a season ago, was already on the table like a glove nobody had found the courage to lift. On Friday she asked, instead, a question, one apiece, of the four. She asked each patroness to name, aloud, for the room's records, the service to Town by which her own family had earned its place inside these walls, and she waited. She is very old, gentle reader, and entirely blind, and she waited the way the river waits, and the room discovered that of its four answers, two were trade dressed as lineage, one was lineage dressed as trade, and one, offered last and very quietly, was a grandfather's commission in the granary corps, at which the Dowager nodded and said, that is the door, my dear. The rest of us climbed through windows and have been redecorating ever since.

The vote followed as arithmetic follows. As for the candidate: he was at his scales by four the next morning, has declined the voucher with thanks, and is reported to have observed that the fish would not weigh themselves. The refreshments of Almeow's are therefore safe from him, and he from them, and this authoress notes for the archive what the room has not yet understood it conceded: the question is inside the walls now. It was carried in on a Friday, by seven ladies and one glove, and no vote to come will ever carry it out.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 34: On Second Chances
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Two numbers ago this paper declined to co-sign a verdict and left its book open on a certain waterlogged young lord. The book closes this week, in the paper's favour, and the ton is invited to observe how the sum was made whole, because the workings are more instructive than the answer.

The young lord did not petition his guardian, did not enlist his friends, did not, wonder of the age, write to anybody. He presented himself instead, at six in the morning, to the keepers of the Saucerine, and asked for a rake. This authoress is informed that the hat was recovered Tuesday, the boat-boy's pole Wednesday, the tablecloths made good at rates that acknowledged the difference between an accident and an inconvenience, and an apology delivered where apologies are hardest and count most, by name, to a working boy, in front of the boy's master. I am further informed, by the kind of channels the ton does not believe I have, that the accounts east of the fountain were closed, paid, and annotated before the west end had finished drafting its regrets, which is, gentle reader, the correct order of solvency, and the only one this paper has ever trusted.

His Excellency, meanwhile, has kept the hat as recovered, wet side out, on a stand in the embassy hall, where he shows it to visitors as, his phrase, the season's finest trophy of the chase. The young lord dines there Thursday. The ton, which had him ruined a fortnight ago, is already re-inviting him with the special warmth it reserves for cats it feels guilty about, and he is accepting with the good grace of a boy who has learned, at nineteen and at rake's length, the season's most expensive lesson: that Town forgives a splash, gentle reader, and remembers a repair.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 35: The Arithmetic Arrives
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

Two years ago this paper began asking a question of natural history about a certain magnificent coat. One year ago it asked more pointedly. Six numbers ago it left its card. This week, the arithmetic arrives, and it arrives, as long arithmetic always does in Mayfur, wearing herring.

The facts as they may be printed. The house of Manxfield holds paper of the silver house's, quantity understated by every version in circulation, and the season of patient purchase is over: notices have gone where notices go, through attorneys of the unhurried kind, and the ton's arithmeticians, who can spot a foreclosure through three brick walls and a dinner service, have priced the outcome and begun composing their condolences, which in Mayfur are indistinguishable from invitations.

What the arithmeticians have not priced, because they cannot see it from the west, is the second column. This paper has written before of ledgers east of the wall, of interest that is not paid in coin, and of feathers finer than any visible diet explains. It repeats none of it today, and adds one sentence only, for subscribers who know how to read a balance: when two creditors hold one asset, gentle reader, the question is never which of them collects. The question is what the asset does when it discovers it was never the debtor. It was the security.

The season has three weeks to run. The paper is at home, as it announced last month, and remains so, and its door, unlike some, has never once been mistaken for a wall.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 36: The Number I Am Glad to Run
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

For two years this paper has kept a file it expected to close in ruin, and this authoress will confess, now that the expectation is dead, that she had the ruinous number half composed. It goes unprinted. What happened instead happened Monday, at Manxfield, before some forty witnesses, and deserves better type than ruin ever gets.

The father rose, took from his strongbox the three notes the whole town has wagered on, and gave them, without one word, to his daughter. The daughter, whose curtsey to a certain lordship was once complimented seam by seam in these pages, and this paper knew what it was reporting even if the room did not, took her ally by the paw, and the two ladies, wronged in parallel and merged into the season's one indissoluble institution, walked the notes to the fire and fed them in, and Miss Bobtail said, to the room, in the voice her family reserves for weights and measures: we have discussed what his lordship's fourteen generations are worth, and have decided we should all rather learn what he is worth without them. He owes us nothing. He never did. The debt was always somebody else's idea of what we were owed.

Mayfur, gentle reader, did not recover its conversation for ten minutes, and this paper has confirmed the interval with three watches.

What the fire ends, the ton can count: a foreclosure, a season's wagering, and the most patient revenge in the herring trade's history, converted at the last instant into something the herring trade has no word for and the paper does: mercy, spent, not sold. What the fire begins is his lordship's own business, conducted, the paper hears, at his own gate, at dawn, with his own paw, and Town will see the sum of it when he chooses to be seen, and not one Wednesday before. Some accounts, this paper has always held, are settled in rooms. The best ones, it learns this week, are settled in fires.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 37: The Diamond, Decided
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

At Wednesday's ball, between the second dance and the supper interval, the patronesses did the thing they have declined all season to do, and did it, this paper must record, with the timing of professionals who have been enjoying themselves: the diamond of the season is Miss Marigold, ward of Blackfriars, of Foldingworth Farm, of the ruby ribbon, and of, this paper's files being what they are, the most patiently constructed campaign since the blockade winter.

The room's eyes went where the room's eyes go, and Her Highness, who has held the title since the day she arrived and defended it precisely never, received the news with the perfect stillness of a cat receiving confirmation, inclined her head to the new diamond by exactly the degree the occasion required, and not a fraction that could be quoted against her, and resumed her conversation with the Ambassador in the delegation's own tongue.

Thursday morning, gentle reader, a single lilac bloom was delivered to the west side of the Square. No card. Town has produced eleven readings of it by Friday, each more certain than the last. This paper offers none. It reports only that the new diamond placed the bloom in water, in her own window, facing the Square, where it stands this morning, and that the two finest campaigners in Mayfur appear to be the only two cats in it who require no translation.

The wager book at Brindle's settled at sums the committee has asked this paper not to print, and this paper, feeling the season has been hard enough on that institution, complies. The knot of a certain ribbon was observed Wednesday night to be a plain bow, daily wear, all quiet. The connoisseurs are invited to consider what it means when the signal flags come down, and the fleet, gentle reader, is still moving.

Yours in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN

entities.title: Society Papers, No. 38: The Season Closes Its Book
entities.content:
Gentle reader,

The knockers come off this week, and the season, which began with seventeen pearls at an opening ball, ended Wednesday with an entrance this paper has waited two years to report without knowing it.

Lord Fluffington came to the last ball shorn. Clipped to the plain grey cat that fourteen generations of silver had been standing on all along, wearing one good coat of the woven kind, correctly cut and nothing more, and he walked into Almeow's the way cats walk into cold water: all at once, having decided. The room took its breath. And then, gentle reader, the room, which has spent two seasons pricing that cat's plumage and one week rehearsing its condescension, surprised itself, as rooms occasionally and redeemingly do: somewhere near the mantel a paw began to tap, another took it up, and what moved through that ballroom was not applause exactly, Almeow's does not applaud, but the sound a wall makes when it decides, all in one moment, to be a door.

He danced once, with Miss Longwhisker, who asked him, the whole room straining and this paper's sources better than the room's, how he did, and received the answer the season will be remembered by: lighter, madam, and learning the weather. The Duchess departs for the country a week early, taking, her household confirms, the old portrait, and leaving, this paper suspects, a version of her son she had not met before Wednesday. The wagering interest, denied its crash, has opened a book on his prospects, and the paper notes with professional pleasure that the odds are kind.

The accounting, then, while the truth is warm. One diamond passed, gracefully. One wall breached, permanently, on a Friday, by one glove. One young lord sunk and refloated inside a fortnight. Two ladies who fed a fortune to a fire and improved on it. One coat converted into a cat. And two account books, gentle reader, ruled off on a town that believes, as it packs its trunks, that it has kept its secrets, an opinion this paper has never once corrected and never once shared.

The wheel comes around, my dears. Be interesting the third time.

Until the spring, in perfect confidence,
LADY WHISKERDOWN
